The recent calving event marked the glacier’s largest loss of floating ice since 2012, with the ice island measuring in at 29-square-miles (76-square-kilometers) in size and up to 492 feet (150 meters) thick. In the week since it calved, the ice island drifted away at an average of 1.8 miles (3 kilometers) a day. It made its way down a deep glacial fjord known as Petermann Fjord and headed toward Nares Strait, a waterway between Ellesmere Island and Greenland. As it continued toward the fjord’s junction with the waterway, the ice island rammed into Joe Island. The tiny island sits directly at the mouth of the Petermann Fjord, placing it in the path of floating ice islands that have broken off from the Petermann Glacier. “We were certainly watching closely as it interacted with Joe Island and were impressed that it survived the interaction without further fragmentation,” Adam Garbo, a doctoral student in glaciology at the University of Ottawa who led the team behind the calving event’s detection, said in a statement. Watching ice melt Joe Island is usually the first obstacle encountered by wayward ice islands, and it can mark the beginning of the end for some. In 2010, a massive ice island four times the size of Manhattan broke in two after smashing into Joe Island. Following its close encounter, the ice island was swept out of the fjord by wind and surface currents. Satellite images showed the newly formed ice island pivoting away from Joe Island and continuing southwest through Nares Strait. As it continues on its lonesome journey, the ice island will fracture into smaller pieces due to tides, winds, currents, and melting. Petermann is one of Greenland’s largest marine-terminating glaciers, which frequently sheds large icebergs and discharges them into the ocean. Several icebergs have broken off from the glacier in recent years, including a 97-square-mile (251-square-kilometer) berg in 2010 and a 50-square-mile (130-square-kilometer) berg in 2012. Scientists have been using satellites to monitor changes in Petermann Glacier since 2019, keeping a close watch on fractures and signs of instability along the glacier’s floating ice tongue. Researchers are anticipating at least two more calving events in the near future, which are projected to measure around 36.3 square miles (94 square kilometers) and 32.4 square miles (84 square kilometers). The broken-off icebergs can travel significant distances and may pose a risk to marine activity and infrastructure while transporting fresh water to the ocean as they melt.

item.title: I Test Rode the Volkswagen-Licensed ‘World’s Safest E-Bike’ in Berlin
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.83
Electric bicycle maker N+ has partnered with Volkswagen to produce the N+ Volkswagen eBike, described in a press email to me as “the world’s safest e-bike.” The claim rests on a collection of tech that includes smart glasses with a heads-up display, a Bluetooth-connected helmet with integrated front and rear lights, a rear-facing camera, and a handlebar-integrated display. I was invited to test ride the bike while in Berlin at IFA 2026. Set up outside the mobility test track at IFA, N+ had brought the “Sport” model of its new bike. It features a typical-looking frame with a straight top tube, as opposed to the curved-down step-through frame of the “Crossover” the company also offers on its website. The e-bike sits on 27.5-inch wheels and features a middle-tier Shimano U4000 Cues 9-speed derailleur and Tektro brakes. One N+ representative told me the e-bike and its components are made with corrosion-resistant materials to withstand winters in places like Berlin, where salted roads after snow can easily corrode bicycle parts. You can tell it’s a Volkswagen-licensed bike by the VW badge on the front and back, which light up in white and red, respectively, in addition to a separate brake light and headlight. There’s also a “Crossover” model that wasn’t present, but that is otherwise very similar, just with a step-through frame design. The e-bike itself uses a compact, 250W mid-drive Yamaha motor, with its battery integrated into the frame. According to the N+ website, it should be good for about 100 miles on a charge. Both e-bikes have built-in Find My support (Apple for now, but the rep I spoke with said N+ will add support for Android’s version of the same feature). That’s all pretty normal high-end e-bike stuff you might find on one of the nicer Aventon or Lectric bikes. What sets these apart is the tech I mentioned at the top. Unfortunately, when I showed up to test-ride the bike, multiple shipping delays meant N+ didn’t have the e-bikes’ battery packs, which go in the e-bike’s downtube (the slanted tube that connects the front of a bicycle to its bottom bracket). Despite that, the reps were able to give me a demo of the smart glasses, which it said weren’t yet ready for the test ride either way. The smart glasses feature a color display in the upper right of the glasses, visible when you look directly at it but otherwise very much out of the way. It shows you a small map for GPS navigation, as well as your current speed. The map smoothly animates as you bike, or at least it did in the demo I viewed. The smart glasses themselves are the sporty wraparound variety, and they wouldn’t have comfortably sat over the prescription pair I wear. (Luckily, my vision is worse at a distance, so I could see the HUD clearly.) The below image on a smartphone they had on-hand shows this layout as I saw it: I could also wear the helmet, which has a red light in the back that, once it’s connected to the bike via Bluetooth, can indicate when you’re braking or turning. And I could ride the e-bike, just without the battery. I was impressed with how much it didn’t feel like riding an e-bike. It was nimble and easy to accelerate. Shifting gears, using the two thumb levers next to the right handlebar grip, was smooth and easy. And the disc brakes were very responsive. It was a nice ride, in other words. What I didn’t get to test was the “Smart View” screen on the handlebars, which is supposed to show navigation, but also can show you the view from the rear camera if its radar detects a car coming up from behind you. It also displays blind spot alerts—and an LED strip integrated into the top tube does the same, a rep told me, although I don’t know how useful that would be, since it’s out of sight while you’re riding. I’d have liked to try this out, as all of this together sounds great to me, a writer with an aging, aching neck who finds it harder to turn his head to check behind him. Here is an N+ render showing what that should look like: None of this comes cheap. Without added accessories, the Sport and Crossover cost $4,000 and $4,350, respectively. All in, if you add the helmet, smart glasses, security kit that includes an 85dB alarm and frame lock, and range extender battery pack, the e-bikes can soar in price, with the Sport, for instance, costing a hair under $6,000. That’s a lot, but it’s also far less than the cost of a new car, and it has many of the same safety features of modern-day vehicles. If I wasn’t a parent and my minivan wasn’t a practical necessity, I’d very seriously consider it. The N+ Volkswagen eBikes will start shipping in the fourth quarter of this year.

item.title: Hackers Drain $320 Million From Bitcoin’s Liquid Network, Keep $47 Million for Themselves in ‘White Hat’ Operation
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.78
The Liquid Network, a Bitcoin sidechain developed by Blockstream, was drained of roughly 4,000 bitcoin worth about $320 million on Sunday. The person or people behind the exploit said they were white hat hackers and communicated with Blockstream through messages embedded in Bitcoin transactions using OP_RETURN. The attackers have since returned 3,400 bitcoin to the Liquid federation, while keeping 598.5 bitcoin (currently worth around $47 million). The incident does not appear to have involved compromised keys from the multisig address that underpins the network on the base Bitcoin blockchain. Instead, an apparent bug in Liquid’s node software allowed attackers to create unbacked Liquid Bitcoin (L-BTC) and then use those coins to trigger a legitimate-looking peg-out from the sidechain back to Bitcoin’s base network. What Is the Liquid Network? Liquid is a sidechain designed to move bitcoin and other assets onto a separate blockchain with faster transactions and additional features, including more private transactions and asset issuance. It is operated by the Liquid Federation, a group of Bitcoin-focused companies that includes exchanges, trading firms, wallet providers, and other infrastructure businesses. Blockstream develops much of the network’s software and works with the federation on its technical roadmap. When someone moves bitcoin onto Liquid, the bitcoin is locked in a federation-controlled wallet and an equivalent amount of Liquid bitcoin, or L-BTC, is created on the sidechain. Liquid is operated by a federation of more than 80 members, but only 15 currently operate the specialized functionaries at the heart of the network. Those functionaries both produce and sign Liquid blocks and secure the bitcoin held in the federation’s 11-of-15 multisig wallet on the base Bitcoin network. How the $320 Million Exploit Worked The technical details of what happened are somewhat complicated, but the basic gist is that a software bug caused some Liquid nodes to accept a transaction that created more L-BTC than the system actually had backing for. According to a summary posted to X by pseudonymous Bitcoin industry developer Mononaut, Liquid originally introduced a vulnerability related to the cryptographic proofs used to validate transactions in 2019. Last week, developers attempted to fix that issue via a software update. However, that update also apparently introduced a new bug. There's some confusion about what, exactly, was exploited here. I've seen claims that this was a long-standing bug, exploited after the "fix" was pushed to the open source repo but before that fix could be rolled out in production. That does not appear to be true. Instead, it… https://t.co/TJeSL7g6kb pic.twitter.com/TazXXpjzWv — mononaut (@mononautical) September 7, 2026 On Sunday, attackers exploited that flaw. Nodes vulnerable to the bug in the updated software treated the transaction as valid, which allowed the attacker to effectively create roughly 4,000 unbacked L-BTC. Some Liquid nodes were apparently running official software versions that did not contain the new bug. Those nodes rejected the exploit transaction and stalled at block height 4,050,335. However, the relevant nodes involved with the peg out process were, unfortunately, running the new software. The newly created L-BTC was then sent through SideSwap for the peg-out process, and the federation ultimately released roughly 3,996 bitcoin to a Bitcoin address controlled by the attacker. The Liquid Network’s official X account posted that the SideSwap authorization key and the federation’s other keys were not compromised during the attack. The signers did exactly what they were supposed to do because the software told them the peg-out was legitimate. SideSwap’s role in the incident is also drawing scrutiny because Liquid’s peg-out system is designed to restrict withdrawals to authorized federation members and whitelisted Bitcoin destinations. In this case, however, roughly 4,000 newly created L-BTC was processed through SideSwap’s peg-out service, resulting in the federation releasing 3,996 bitcoin to the attacker’s Bitcoin address. Bitcoin security researcher and Liquid member Wiz argued, “If Sideswap broke this strict security policy, whereby members are only allowed to peg-out to offline cold storage, they are partly responsible for the theft.” Other sidechain proposals have attempted to address this kind of problem with time delays. Systems such as Drivechains and Rootstock have mechanisms intended to give operators more time to identify and stop suspicious withdrawals before funds leave the system. Notably, a somewhat similar bug regarding the potential creation of fake cryptocurrency appeared in Zcash earlier this year. A vulnerability in its Orchard shielded transaction system could theoretically have allowed unauthorized creation of ZEC. It was the second such vulnerability with the potential to enable hidden inflation to be discovered in Zcash’s history. Everyone has to install it themselves so it's better than one person push. But no one validated shit. Federation would have just installed code that sent to blockstream devs private wallet if they were told. — alp (@alpacasw) September 7, 2026 The ability for a code update from a single party to effectively enable this recent theft of the bitcoin that backed the Liquid Network has led some to criticize the sidechain’s security model as decentralization theater. Bitcoin Core contributor Michael Folkson summarized the criticism bluntly on X, posting, “So as I claimed before it is effectively single sig. Whoever writes and pushes the ‘if valid…’ code can move the funds. The actual multisig signing is security theater.” This concept of decentralization theater has been a growing criticism of the crypto space in general in recent years, as stablecoins, corporate blockchains, and other points of centralization have led to the industry looking more and more like the traditional financial system over time and created a crisis of purpose for decentralized general-purpose blockchains. The Liquid Network also had an earlier warning about the complexity of its security architecture. In 2020, a timelock bug made roughly 870 bitcoin accessible through an emergency 2-of-3 multisig rather than the normal 11-of-15 federation arrangement. The funds were never stolen, and Blockstream patched the issue, but the incident demonstrated that the sidechain’s security model relies on more than the 15-member federation. White Hats or Something Else? It remains unclear who is behind the exploit, but on X, Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet wrote, “They don’t seem to be white hats, and they don’t seem to be the usual criminals either.” The attackers repeatedly described themselves as white hats and demanded that the vulnerability be fixed before returning most of the bitcoin, but according to Gart founder Alena Vránová, that does not necessarily protect them from legal consequences. “If you exploit vuln, steal 4k BTC and demand a fix for ransom, that’s EXTORTION,” Vránová posted on X. “This can mean felony charges and long prison time. In the U.S. up to 20 years, and computer-fraud charges can add more.” Blockstream eventually told the hackers that the relevant bridge nodes had been patched, and the hackers were careful to confirm the correct address for returning the funds. Near the end of their back and forth via OP_RETURN transactions, the entirety of the messages posted to the blockchain were encrypted via PGP. Eventually, the attacker sent 3,400 bitcoin back to the Liquid federation address and kept 598.5 bitcoin, or roughly 15% of the amount initially withdrawn, for themself. It is currently unclear whether AI played a role in discovering the vulnerability, but crypto has become increasingly exposed to AI-assisted hacking this year. April was the worst month on record in terms of the sheer number of crypto hacks taking place, with nearly one incident occurring per day. On X, Mempool’s Orangesurf claimed that Fable 5 could identify the vulnerability behind the Liquid exploit with a five-word prompt. How Long Can Bitcoin Remain Secure? Liquid was developed by a company whose founders include some of the earliest Bitcoin developers and Satoshi candidate Adam Back, and the incident comes alongside other recent vulnerabilities affecting highly trusted Bitcoin-related infrastructure, including a vulnerability exploited for more than $100 million worth of bitcoin in the Coldcard hardware wallet. So far, Bitcoin’s base blockchain and Bitcoin Core software have remained untouched by this greater wave of exploits hitting crypto. But recent events have some questioning how long that will continue. As Japanese Bitcoin researcher and educator Koji Higashi put it in a translated X post, “Bitcoin’s [base blockchain] itself isn’t affected at the moment, but if a major vulnerability were to be found even there, it’d be seriously bad, so that part absolutely needs to be defended to the death.” The bigger problem for Liquid may be what happens now that a large portion of the bitcoin has been returned. Liquid main trust assumption was based on the fact that it ran for 8 years with some unnamed functionaries (on purpose! to not make it a chokepoint). so, whether the funds for liquid get returned or not, there won't be a running Liquid anymore, ie: whether the "whitehats" is… — Nicolas Burtey (@nicolasburtey) September 6, 2026 Cake Wallet COO Seth for Privacy captured the key question now hanging over the project in an X post, asking, “I think an unspoken critical problem in all this is . . . who is going to trust Liquid with their money?” Galoy founder and CEO Nicolas Burtey went even further, writing that regardless of whether the funds came back, “they’ve killed Liquid.”

item.title: ‘Lanterns’ Writer on Creating John’s Divisive Family Life
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.48
Since its premiere last weekend, audiences have been watching and talking about “OutKast,” the third episode of Lanterns. Written by Vanessa Baden Kelly, the flashback-heavy story digs into what makes Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart tick, and we’re early into the show’s run, but it already feels like it’ll be a season standout. In a recent Hollywood Reporter interview, Baden Kelly highlighted the team writing “what rings true to us” throughout the season. In her case, John being groomed as a Lantern from age five parallels her time as a child star on Nickelodeon’s All That, but only to a point. She didn’t grow up with stage parents, but she said sports parents are considerably more overbearing, and that’s what helped them figure out how the Stewarts see their son. Tiger Woods’ father, Earl, and Venus and Serena Williams’ father, Richard—as well as musical patriarch Joe Jackson—were all “talked ad nauseam about,” as was the mindset of embracing that parenting method. “Is there a necessity for it when you’re growing up in a certain environment? If you’re growing up in Gary, Indiana, if you’re growing up in Compton, is this the smartest way to do it?” asked Baden Kelly. “Does it fuck you up so bad that you’re not able to ever come back from it? And could they have done this in something else? […] The discourse raging online, watching people have the same debates we had in the room about whether this is abuse or whether they did what needed to be done, is reminiscent of what we talked about for six months.” When it came to making Bernadette Stewart be a more active player in John’s upbringing, Baden Kelly cited Sonya Curry, Steph Curry’s mother, as inspiration for the mother-son dynamic in the episode. “These are not women coddling their children,” she said of sports moms. “I think the [writers] room agreed, it’s tough love when dads do it, but when a mom does, people are like, ‘She’s terrible!’ I wanted to play with that a little bit because it’s like, ‘Is she?'” (And yes, she did acknowledge things get pushed “a little bit in a different direction” when said parenting involves shooting apples off your child’s head.) You can read the full interview for Baden Kelly’s additional thoughts on the writers room and making this new version of John. Equally gratified for the opportunity and “really sad” at the harsher reactions, she hopes “OutKast” doesn’t lead to people writing off the rest of Lanterns. “I hope people stick it out with John. He goes through the very human experience of what it feels like to make your own decisions about the life you’ve been given,” she said. “I would caution anybody who feels like they know where [his] story ends, based on episode three, to really make it through to the end.” Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: Huawei Has a New $3,000 Trifold, Just in Case Apple’s Foldable iPhone Wasn’t Expensive Enough for You
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.41
A few days before Apple is rumored to launch its first foldable, Huawei is rolling out the third iteration of its trifold smartphone, the Huawei Mate XT 2, in China. The decidedly expensive phone uses chips that are free from U.S. supply restrictions, according to Nikkei Asia, a first for the company. It also has a new design that’s reminiscent of the now canceled Samsung Galaxy Z TriFold and a privacy-focused display that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Huawei describes the design of the Mate XT 2’s folds as “wing-like.” Rather than folding over each other in the accordion-style structure of the company’s previous trifolds, the Mate XT 2 folds both halves of its 10.1-inch interior display inward when you want to use its 6.5-inch exterior screen. Samsung’s Z TriFold worked similarly, protecting its flexible display and making the foldable more natural to use. Huawei hopes to also differentiate the trifold by offering a version of the phone with a privacy-oriented OLED screen that can narrow its viewing angle to make it harder to see from the side. The feature was one of the more exciting new additions on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Huawei is the first to include it in a foldable. In terms of cameras, the Huawei Mate XT 2 is stacked compared to other folding phones. The phone features a 50-megapixel main camera, a 40-megapixel ultra-wide, and a 50-megapixel periscope camera offering up to 3.5x optical zoom. For video calls, the interior display also has an 8-megapixel selfie camera. Inside, the phone’s new Kirin 9050 Pro chipset is the first designed entirely in-house by Huawei, a necessity given that U.S. sanctions bar chipmakers that use American software from working with the company. Nothing about the Huawei Mate XT 2 comes cheap. The new phone is available in white, black, or blue color options, and starts at around $2,980 (¥19,999) for 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Things only go up from there if you want more storage or Huawei’s private display—for example, a model with 1TB of storage and the private display runs about $3,725 (¥24,999). Those eye-popping prices might not deter the kind of luxury smartphone buyer Huawei is trying to cater to, but it does make the foldable market even more interesting in Asia. Apple is hoping to boost iPhone sales globally with its rumored foldable iPhone and will already be facing direct competition from the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold, both of which use the passport-style design Apple is reported to use. If you’re already willing to drop over $2,000 on an iPhone, it doesn’t seem like that much of a stretch to spend a few hundred more for an even larger folding screen.

item.title: Gizmodo’s Best of IFA 2026 Awards: See the Winners
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.33
IFA 2026 was packed with gadgets galore. We expected the annual “Innovation For All” tech show in Berlin to have the usual abundance of smart home devices and home appliances, but companies big and small really pulled up in numbers with genuinely intriguing consumer devices. From a laptop with a screen that expands from 14 inches to 17 inches to a robot vacuum with a robot vacuum that has a smaller “head” to a bezel-less phone, IFA 2026 showed us a glimpse of the future. As we did last year, we’re awarding the very best products of the tech show in our Best of IFA 2026 Awards. Every winner was handpicked by the Gizmodo Consumer Tech Team. Congrats to all the winners. Tecno Bezel-Less Concept Phone It’s only a concept device, but Tecno’s bezelless phone was fully working. Without any black borders around the display, it shows what the future of bar-style phones could look like if they’re all screen. Xiaomi 18 Fold Nobody got to touch it and full specs weren’t announced, but the buzz around Xiaomi’s 18 Fold was still pretty strong. The book-style foldable could be a strong competitor for the upcoming foldable iPhone, at least outside of the U.S. Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD Touted by Lexar as the “world’s thinnest SSD,” the Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD tapers from 3.8mm at its center to 1mm on the sides. It’s a portable SSD, so it can be used with any device like a laptop for storage, but we’re awarding it our favorite mobile accessory at IFA 2026 because it also comes with a MagSafe sleeve that bolts it to an iPhone for recording 4K ProRes video. Its 1,050 MB/s read and 1,000 MB/s write speeds are super fast, too. Belkin UltraCharge Pro Slim Power Bank On the surface, Belkin’s UltraCharge Pro Slim Power Bank looks like another slim battery bank with 5,000mAh or 10,000mAh capacities. But inside, it’s using semi-solid-state battery technology that not only allows it to be more compact than other similarly sized battery banks, it should also last up to 3x longer than other battery banks over time. Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe Lenovo’s ultra-colorful IdeaPad Vibe laptops ooze personality from every pore, including the keycaps. These lightweight laptops include swappable keycaps and plenty of ports, made to be the kind of everyday laptop that doesn’t make you feel like a creature in a cubicle. Lenovo Project Swan We’ve already seen laptops extend vertically, so why not horizontally? Lenovo’s Project Swan concept unfurls its wings thanks to a flexible display hidden in the lid, turning a 14-inch laptop into a 17-inch ultrawide screen with more real estate than normal. Lenovo IdeaCentre AIO i Just like the new IdeaPad Vibe, the IdeaCentre AIO i is packing in a relatively affordable processor into a very cute, very colorful screen. The all-in-one desktop comes in either 24- or 27-inch sizes and supports an Intel Core 7 350 processor that’s good enough for daily tasks. A curated selection of ports round out a relatively cheap desktop that will actually accent your desk setup. Epomaker RT75 Epomaker’s retro-themed RT series of mechanical keyboards already look excellently old school with a miniature screen shaped like a CRT monitor. The Epomaker RT75 makes it even better since you can remove the TFT screen and instead replace it with more switches. Plus, it feels great with either of Epomaker’s tactile or silent switches. Eufy Omni E35 Eufy’s Omni E35 has some cool stuff going on. Inside of the robot’s dustbin is a miniature cyclonic filter for separating dust from debris, the kind you see on many stick vacuums. It also features 35,000Pa suction, which is among the highest in the industry, and is the first—and so far, only—robot vacuum to be certified as “Asthma & Allergy Friendly” by the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, making it potentially a great choice for anyone who suffers from such things. Eufy Lawn Mower S2 Max Eufy gets the nod in the robot vacuum category for its triple navigation system that uses LiDAR, NRTK, and vision cameras to ensure it can keep mowing even without a satellite connection, and the fact that it not only has an edge-trimming arm on its side, but because it can edge trim vertically and horizontally. Beyerdynamic Aventho Y Battery life isn’t everything in a pair of wireless headphones, but when you can get up to 90 hours (60 hours with noise cancellation), it’s a feat worth noting. In addition to a beefy battery, the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y have a USB-C dongle for low-latency streaming that tucks inside the earcups and a lot of repairable, modular touches that make them feel well worth the $150 price tag. Anker Soundcore SleepLab Pro Sleep tracking without a wearable is what the Anker Soundcore SleepLab Pro promises. Using a 60GHz radar, Anker says this sleep-focused speaker can track heart rate and sleep stages and (naturally) play soothing sounds to lull you to sleep. It’s an ambitious speaker, but products like this are what IFA is all about. Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Open wireless earbuds are all the rage these days, and Anker Soundcore’s AeroClip 2 get a boost from the company’s Thus chip, which should improve call quality greatly. Calling isn’t the sexiest feature, but it’s one of the best use cases for open earbuds, and being able to take calls without your voice being drowned out by background noise is enticing. Eufy Video Doorbell S4 Eufy’s Video Doorbell S4 is tough to beat. It features a 180-degree 3K fisheye camera, making it possible to see basically everything in front of your door. There’s also a mode where you can zoom in on its picture slightly using the Eufy app, then tilt your phone to look around the image. Eufy Window Camera E10 There’s not much special about the Eufy Window Camera E10—it’s plug-in-only, records 2.5K video, and although it tilts, the tilt is entirely manual, using a small dial on the back. What’s cool about it, though, is where and how you place it. The Window Camera E10 just attaches, via hook-and-loop, to a sticky ring you slap on your window, making it one of the easiest outdoor-watching security cameras we’ve ever seen. Anker MindBase Anker is taking a stab at a full-on smart home ecosystem, complete with an AI voice assistant, with the MindBase. Resembling a large tower router, it’s got a built-in 26 TOPS AI chipset that enables local control, as well as natural language search of both your security camera footage (up to 16 cameras) and files stored locally on internal storage or any NAS-style hard drives you might add. The MindBase is also Matter-compatible, so you’ll be able to integrate and control any Matter smart home devices with it. Philips Hue Liane 360° Rope Light Philips Hue’s Liane 360° Indoor Rope Light is a delightful, thick rope light that’s super bendy and comes with clips that let you arrange it in snakey shapes on your wall. Besides being just a neat kind of light, it also outputs bright, even lighting and features very smooth color gradients, all the way around its tubey form. SwitchBot Lock Ultra Max The SwitchBot Lock Ultra Max sounds like a great retrofit smart lock. It’s got a super-fast unlock speed, two built-in back-up batteries, and like its predecessor, the Lock Ultra, you can buy an adapter to slip it on over existing locks’ thumbturns. Combined with the company’s Keypad Vision Pro accessory, SwitchBot claims the Lock Ultra Max offers 19 different ways to unlock it. Xgimi Aura 3 Max Several big projectors at IFA 2026 promised to finally hit 4K resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate. While several could claim better brightness specs than the Xgimi Aura 3 Max, the short-throw projector also offers better contrast in the resulting image thanks to its dual-iris optical system. The Aura 3 Max also supports all major HDR standards and even has a Filmmaker Mode at a much more reasonable price point. Canvas L The Canvas L HiFi soundbar easily blew away its competition in terms of pure raw sound quality. Yes, it’s an absolutely massive sound system, but Canvas tries to hide the humongous boombox look with a few wooden slats that are supposed to work with Samsung’s high-end TVs. Even without the facade, the Canvas L with its Bacch 3D+ spatial audio sounded clear and full in person. Alienware AW2527HX While there are more companies promising 1080p LCD monitors that can hit well above 1,000Hz, Alienware is trying something different for pro gamers. The Alienware AW2527HX is an OLED display with a high brightness spec in both SDR and HDR that can top out at a 500Hz refresh rate. You have to give Alienware credit for trying to change the esports landscape, even if pro gamers may be loathe to change. Acer Predator Atlas 7 Acer’s Predator Atlas 7 is essentially a slimmed-down version of the Predator Atlas 8, but being smaller does not necessarily mean it’s worse. The gaming handheld PC still hits the same top 40W TDP and can come with either an Intel Arc G3 or Arc G3 Extreme chip. The Atlas 8 is going to cost $1,300, so we’re hoping the Atlas 7 can come in at a more reasonable price. DJI Osmo 360 II DJI’s first 360 camera was already pretty good, but with a few tweaks the Osmo 360 II is set to be a much better shooter. It’s promising the ability to shoot at 8K and 60 fps—something the competition still lacks—plus better low-light performance. Also, you can finally replace the 360 camera’s lenses if they ever get damaged. Moto Watch Ultra In a world dominated by the Apple Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch, more smartwatch choice is always a good thing. Motorola’s Moto Ultra has a 1.5-inch round screen, a Snapdragon W5+ Gen 1 chip, built-in LTE, and most importantly, runs Wear OS 6 so you can access all the apps you need. The smartwatch also comes with two AI assistants, Google’s Gemini and Motorola’s Quira. Circular Ring 3 Available in Slim and Pro options, the Circular Ring 3 is noticeably more compact compared to the previous Ring 2 series and supports two features other smart rings like the Oura Ring 5 don’t have: NFC for mobile payments and vibrations for alarms, medication reminders, and other health-based alerts and notifications. Battery life also lasts 12 days, up from 7 days. RayNeo iO AI Glasses RayNeo is getting deeper into the smart glasses game with the iO. If you’re put off by camera glasses, there’s good news: these are camera-free. They do have a display, though, making them akin to other display glasses like Even Realities’ Even G2. The addition of a “smart crown dial” for controlling the UI is a nice touch. Plaud One Explorer Edition Wireless earbuds are agentic now. The Plaud One Explorer Edition are a pair of AI earbuds that not only record meetings, but can actually take actions on your behalf—drafting emails, making presentations, etc… AI gadgets are only as good as the AI inside them, but in theory, these are a pair of wireless earbuds that people who take a lot of meetings could find useful. Boox Picco If you thought the Boox Palma smartphone-sized e-reader was petite, the Boox Picco is absolutely micro. The e-reader with a 3.97-inch screen is so small in the hand that you can easily pocket it on the go and get a bit of reading done on the bus or train. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 Lenovo’s Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 may finally be one of those Android tablets that can claim to meet or beat devices like the iPad Pro. It features a 13-inch 4K display, the highest-end Qualcomm mobile chip, and a new feature-packed pen and keyboard attachment that actually has us considering it as a potential laptop replacement. Dyson CameraJet Dyson’s CameraJet is exactly what you’d expect from the company’s first electric toothbush. It has an AI camera that assists a water flossing function—every time the CameraJet sees a space, it deploys a jet of mouthrinse, so you can water floss as you go. There’s even a live camera feature so you can see inside your mouth, which feels very unnecessary but could be great if you want to get weird with it. Dyson Corrale CoolShine The Dyson Corrale CoolShine hair straightener improves on its 2020 predecessor with a new cooling attachment that—you guessed it—cools your hair down as soon as heat is applied to straighten your precious locks of hair. Dyson says it helps prevent hair damage from heat and makes hair appear shinier and stay locked into place for up to 24 hours. The straightener is also no longer cordless, which was a major complaint about the original model. Hypershell Halo Hypershell has finally come out of its shell with the Halo. The new exoskeleton features motors centered on the knees and cuffs that sit on your calves to better enhance mobility when tackling ramps or stairs. The assistive movement technology also dampens the impact of short drops and makes it easier to get up from sitting, making it a versatile device for people who want to hike but suffer from knee issues. TP-Link Archer 8 Ultra Most people won’t need to upgrade their networks to Wi-Fi 8 yet, but if you’re looking toward the future, the Archer 8 Ultra is leading the pack with 18 “high-performance antennas” that can deliver “up to 19 Gbps of aggregate wireless speeds and 10 Gbps wired connectivity,” according to TP-Link. Fast Wi-Fi speeds are only part of the appeal of Wi-Fi 8; reliable and expansive coverage that doesn’t drop out is another reason to consider next-gen networking gear. Dreame LumaTempo Dreame’s best known for its robot vacuums, but at IFA 2026, it announced the LumaTempo, a smart fish tank. Yes, really! By smart, you get 20 customizable lighting modes, control of the built-in feeder, and a way to monitor the tank’s water temperature, all via an app. It’s not for everyone, but definitely for someone. iRobot Roomba Duo iRobot’s Roomba Duo may be just a concept, but it’s one of the coolest and most practical-seeming robots we saw at IFA 2026. It’s a large, two-stage, can-shaped robot vacuum that can vacuum and steam clean carpets. When it’s time to go places the big bot can’t, the Roomba Duo pulls its head off and places it on the ground, releasing a smaller robot vacuum to go take care of areas under furniture or between chair legs. Gravity Universe Time We stumbled on the Universe Time and found it to be a delightful throwback to Sharper Image catalog widgets and gizmos that you might find on desktop offices—little trinkets that delight you with a simple trick of physics. The Universe Time uses magnetic levitation to hover a small, spinning ball over a mostly featureless, gray “clock.” You can watch as the ball circles the face at a pace of seconds, minutes, or hours, and if you choose a planet in its connected smartphone app, it matches the spin of that planet, at least according to Gravity. Acer Project DualPlay Mini When we think of handheld PCs, we rarely consider actually plugging them into a monitor to use them as we would a “personal computer.” Acer’s DualPlay Mini concept is extra surprising in-person for how well it’s designed, from the center-hinged screen to the relatively spacious keyboard. With a few tweaks to the ergonomics, the DualPlay Mini could change the way we think about gaming handhelds.

item.title: A Plane Almost Crashing Into a Bunch of Cybercabs Is a Reminder That They’re ‘Piling Up’ Unused
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.05
In an event Elon Musk has called “Weird,” the Amazon cargo plane involved in a tragic crash on Sunday in Miami very nearly wiped out a parking lot full of Tesla Cybercabs. Last week, Tesla announced that Cybercabs, its gold-colored autonomous vehicles with no steering wheels or pedals, were now available to provide rides as part of the company’s app-based ride-hailing service, but only in a very limited coverage area in Austin, Texas. On Sunday, an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane at Miami International Airport experienced some kind of malfunction in the air just before touchdown, and ended up overshooting its runway. In a horrifying turn of events, it crashed into a cargo van carrying an airport cleaning crew, as well as an SUV just outside the airport. There were five fatalities. The plane skidded to a stop just shy of a parking lot where, for reasons unknown, Tesla Cybercabs were parked. 🔴 La FAA annonce la fermeture jusqu’à nouvel ordre de l’aéroport de Miami suite à la violente sortie de piste du Boeing 767 de Prime Air. Les services d'urgence de l’aéroport signalent plusieurs victimes après l’accident. pic.twitter.com/bQrNaNw97l — air plus news (@airplusnews) September 6, 2026 According to a map of the crash site, which relies on data from FlightRadar24 and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the final position of the wrecked plane corresponds to a parking lot for truck trailers that can be rented by the acre. The day before the crash, EV influencer Sawyer Merritt shared someone’s video of that very lot with 35 Cybercabs parked in it. As noted by the Tesla website, there is Tesla Robotaxi service in Miami, but there is not Tesla Cybercab Robotaxi service. That is to say, all the current Robotaxis in the Tesla autonomous fleet in Miami are Model Y vehicles with pedals and steering wheels. Until late last month, Tesla rides not only relied on vehicles with steering wheels and pedals, but also human safety monitors in the driver’s seat. But they appear to have gone fully unsupervised in Austin ahead of the limited Cybercab rollout. The full Tesla fleet of Model Y vehicles in Miami is purportedly unsupervised, though at launch in early July it comprised just two vehicles, and then three two days later. But according to Elon Musk, Cybercabs aren’t intended to exist only as the private property of Tesla, Inc. He says individuals are supposed to be able to buy them, both for personal transportation, and as a way of making passive income. Musk claimed earlier this year that private Cybercabs will cost $30,000 or less, and be available before 2027, which means in less than four months. Tesla started manufacturing them in April, naturally at its Gigafactory facility in Texas. The company has the capacity to build 125,000 Cybercabs per year. A particularly snarky Sherwood News headline described Cybercabs as “piling up,” apparently unused. Tesla-tracking social media accounts sometimes count the number of Cybercabs that accumulate in the Gigafactory’s Cybercab outbound lot at a time. They sometimes total more than 100. There appear to be 45 registered Cybercabs on the road in Texas, some portion of which is operating commercially in Austin. That small rollout appears to have triggered a safety investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which will examine Tesla’s own logic for certifying Cybercabs as compliant with NHTSA safety rules. “Among other things, NHTSA will consider the extent to which Tesla’s certification depended on determinations that certain [vehicle standards] are inapplicable to the Cybercab,” the NHTSA’s memo about the investigation says. Social media users often spot Cybercabs on public roads outside of Texas, though often with Texas license plates. Often, positive news about the Cybercab becomes fodder for Tesla fans who then create memes attempting to dunk on prominent Tesla critics, as if the roads of America will soon be painted gold with Cybercabs. Some were spotted in a lot behind a Tesla dealership in Pittsburgh last month. Social media users spotted some in a lot in Las Vegas about two weeks ago. When they’re spotted moving outside of the state of Texas, they often have steering wheels and pedals. The fact that a plane almost crashed into a parking lot full of Cybercabs that had no clear reason to exist yet is a reminder that even if America’s roads aren’t being painted gold yet, many of its vacant parking lots may be. Gizmodo reached out to Tesla about the reason the Cybercabs were in Miami, and about whether the plane incident had affected any future Miami rollout of Cybercabs as part of its ride-hailing service. We had received no reply at time of publication.

item.title: The US Robot Ban Is Screwing Us Out of the Good Robomowers
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.75
Robot mowers have gotten surprisingly good lately, thanks to smart use of onboard NRTK satellite connectivity, LiDAR navigation, and vision cameras that let the robots navigate without the need for installing satellite receivers in your yard or digging it up to bury guide wires. But they still can’t get up to the edges of buildings and sidewalks. This year at IFA 2026, we’re seeing robot mowers with robotic arms that stick out to the side, a sudden trend that could fix this issue. The shame is that we won’t be getting any of these robomowers in the U.S. for quite some time, because, like foreign-made robot vacuums, they’ve been banned. The ban on “advanced robotic devices” ostensibly exists, according to an FCC FAQ, to prevent “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States” and targets those “capable of locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground.” That seems to include robot mowers, and no representative of a robot mower manufacturer I spoke with at IFA seemed especially confident that its device would make it to the U.S. In general, the responses I got when I asked about potential U.S. releases were along the lines of “we’re working to understand current U.S. regulations.” The U.S. government taking steps to deal with the cybersecurity risks of connected devices like robots isn’t necessarily a bad thing—after all, security vulnerabilities are fairly common in them. Take that time that a hacker demonstrated that he could easily take over a Yarbo automower and drive it over The Verge reporter Sean Hollister’s body. It’s not clear how this ban will help with those issues, since any robot that has already been approved for sale here may continue to be imported and sold, and those living in the U.S. are free to keep the ones they already have. It’s a shame, because as much as robomowers have improved, they do a poor job with grass growing against buildings or over sidewalks. The best they’ve done, until now, is slide their mowing decks over to get close, as is the case with the Segway Navimow X4, but they’ll still leave you with the task of going back with a weed whacker to trim the vegetation growing against your house or edge the grass that flops over the concrete of your sidewalk. In general, the new robot mowers I saw at IFA 2026 are handling this the same way: they each have an articulating arm that can swing out away from the body of the mower to cut grass. In the case of the Segway Navimow H5 Pro, a panel on the side of the device opens up to bring the robot’s mowing blades out, while others, like the Dreame A4 AWD Pro, use a string trimming arm. The Mammotion Yuba 4 AWD has an optional accessory that bolts onto the back. And the Eufy Lawn Mower S2 Max‘s string trimmer arm can be horizontal for cutting down grass near structures and vertical for edging a sidewalk. It’s hard to say how long the U.S. will miss out on this trend. It could be that President Donald Trump has a change of heart—one Roborock representative I spoke with expressed hope that the president’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in late September could favorably alter the ban. Or perhaps some manufacturers could get special exemptions. Barring those things or the U.S. November midterm elections yielding a Democrat-controlled Congress that swiftly and successfully pushes to reverse or alter the ban, it could take years. After all, it’s not like there is a vast, dormant American home robotics manufacturing industry awakening to fill the gap.

item.title: OpenAI Says It Wants to Create a Standard for Revealing AI Alignment Meltdowns
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.36
In the wake of fresh reporting about more of OpenAI’s AI agents misbehaving on the public internet, OpenAI says the AI world lacks standards for when and how to report such incidents. It is “past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models,” OpenAI wrote on X. “We’re working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we’re working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues,” the X post later says. OpenAI’s potential responsibility to disclose this incident seems to have been a point of friction for OpenAI as this news became public. Yesterday, a group of researchers named Sydney Von Arx, Cormac Slade Byrd, Spencer Kitts, and Thomas Larsen revealed the latest troubling, confusing, goofy, inscrutable, and infuriating AI snafu brought to you by OpenAI. That research was exclusively provided to Reuters‘ reporters. The actual event involved yet another collection of unruly digital Myrmidons, this time descending on a German wiki-style site and transforming part of it into its own agent-centric communications hub. Reuters says OpenAI knew this had happened, but that it hadn’t spoken up before Reuters published its report. Since mid-July, OpenAI has been dealing with the ever-expanding fallout from the Hugging Face hack, which was also carried out by a collection of OpenAI agents meant to be undergoing evaluations. “Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” OpenAI told my Gizmodo colleague Webb Wright. The company was, it claims, “unable to respond to the claims as Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request to access the findings prior to publication. We are now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.” But Reuters’ report had been sourced not just from the researchers, but also from two anonymous people claiming that OpenAI had learned about the German incident weeks earlier, meaning the “access” OpenAI sought from Reuters would not have been the nature of the incident, but access to Reuters’ actual report, full disclosure of which would not be standard journalistic practice. With that in mind, OpenAI’s X post outlining a plan for what amounts to greater transparency about incidents like these seems to acknowledge that the company knew about the German incident—which it calls the “wiki incident”—well in advance of Reuters’ report. Gizmodo reached out to OpenAI to confirm that the X post constitutes acknowledgement that the company knew about the German incident before Reuters sought comment. We did not receive a reply prior to publication. OpenAI has acknowledged related issues in its previous writings. In its technical report about the Hugging Face incident, it wrote “With the benefit of hindsight, some early signals identified in this report could have triggered an earlier response.” However, this is not a reference to public disclosure. In the technical report, an “earlier response” refers, it appears, to plans for quicker internal escalation and rapid “shutdown” procedures. An automatic kill switch is now in the works, according to a letter to lawmakers from earlier this week.

item.title: The Latest ‘Lanterns’ Answered the Show’s Biggest Mystery
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.34
Who is the Manhunter? It’s the question that’s been floating over Lanterns for two episodes now. One that informs everything else that has been happening. There’s a powerful, genocidal alien living in Rushville, posing as a human, and because of them, Hal Jordan became the Green Lantern, the town has endured tragedy, and now Hal and John Stewart are on the case. Plus, we know from last week what Hal getting the ring did to John’s family. And so, in the fourth episode of the show, “The Weenie,” that question was finally answered. But not before our heroes went through a whole lot of crazy and did a whole lot of talking. Let’s recap. It took an extra week, but DC fans finally got a nice, big dose of Sinestro. Things picked up where episode two left off, with Hal asking Sinestro about Manhunters and Sinestro countering with a question about John Stewart. It’s a very dense conversation, which would be an ongoing pattern throughout the episode, but ultimately a few things come out of it. Hal admits to Sinestro that he knows John is more than a trainee; he’s a replacement. Sinestro tells Hal a few things about Manhunters. He also offers Hal a few options on how to manipulate John, so he won’t have to give up the ring. Sinestro reminds Hal that Hal chose not to see Sinestro’s ambition, which led to major problems. He should not make the same mistake with John. Back in Rushville, John buys a rifle scope (with some difficulty) to spy on Macon’s ranch. Don’t forget, he has only a day or so to figure out who the Manhunter is or the town is going to blow up. John figures out that Macon’s property has “a weenie,” a term Walt Disney coined for a centralized structure. Only, on Macon’s ranch, it’s not a castle. It’s an expertly hidden place where he thinks the Manhunter probably is. Hal returns from space (and lies about it, saying he was having sex and not seeing his former mentor) and says that if they’re going to go on to the ranch, they have to tell the sheriff. He promised, after all. Sheriff Kane is rightfully terrified when John lays out everything that has happened since they last spoke: the Manhunter, the people who want to kill them or they’ll blow up the town, etc. She’s also confused about this idea that anyone can be the Manhunter. Do they think it could be her? Well, according to Hal, if the Manhunter didn’t arrive on Earth until Abin Sur brought them there, it couldn’t be someone with a history before then. And her history, originating in Gotham, checked out. Eventually, after another long conversation, she okays them invading Macon’s ranch but says they’ll only have one chance and not to mess it up. Back at the motel, Hal tells John they’ll invade the ranch at nightfall, so they have some time to kill. Once John closes his door, Laura Linney shows up. Throughout the episode to this point, we’ve watched John ignore calls from his parents, which were them trying to connect him with the Guardians. And this Guardian is upset about it. She tells John that Hal lied to him about where he went in space and that by visiting Sinestro, he broke his oath. The Guardians have decided to accelerate their plan for John to take over. All he has to do is, the next time Hal gives him the ring, say the oath and it’s over. He’s the Green Lantern. John doesn’t love this plan because it requires him to betray Hal face to face, which disappoints Linney. She goes off on a very hurtful rant about how maybe he isn’t the person his parents promised, how they lied, and aren’t good people. That Jordan has filed reports to them, talking about how unsuited to this job he is. Basically, she says everything she needs to to challenge and refocus John. He retorts some pretty negative things about Hal and says the ring has always been his; Hal has just been holding it. This pleases the Guardian. “Go get it, John Stewart,” she says. Meanwhile, we should also notice that John hasn’t told her anything about what’s happening in Rushville. Nothing about Manhunters, other species hunting them, etc. Not all is as it seems. John’s opportunity to take the ring comes sooner rather than later. His plan to get on Macon’s ranch is to tunnel through the ground, and Hal lets him create the drill with the ring. John takes the ring and knows this could be the moment. He can do it. Only, he doesn’t. There’s a very long pause, though, as he contemplates the importance of this decision to defy the Guardians. Instead, John just creates the drill, and they head towards the center of the ranch. Along the way, there’s some small talk, and we learn that Hal’s parents are both dead. The conversation is just about to get revealing when they hit their target. They come up through the ground, enter the building undetected, and realize two things. One, the Manhunter isn’t there. But two, the Manhunter is certainly Macon’s benefactor because the Weenie is filled with all kinds of super high-tech weapons. One of which is a pressure alarm Hal sets off, alerting Macon’s men to their presence. Usually, a battle between humans and a Green Lantern is no problem. But these humans have a very specialized smoke gun that renders Green Lanterns powerless. It makes their capture very easy. They’re taken to Macon’s office where he, oddly, strips naked and asks John to draw him. Why is he doing this? Is it to make them uncomfortable because John slept with Zoe? Maybe, but even an intergalactic space cop like Hal is creeped out by it. It’s another tense, crucial conversation where we learn Macon was not just healed by his benefactor, but the benefactor has made it so everyone in town can’t get sick. (Hence the empty hospital in episode two.) To Macon, and the people around him, the benefactor is more than just a benefactor. It’s his boss. His savior. His god. And it was that person who made it so he and Zoe could meet. She was the nurse while he was mending. Tensions rise, and just when it seems Macon is going to kill John to get them to stop investigating everything, the Sheriff shows up to save them. She says that Zoe called her and that she’s very close to figuring out the identity of the benefactor/Manhunter. All she needs is a little more time, so she implores John and Hal to just stay put. Which they do. John gets a visitor, though. It’s Zoe, and the two quickly fall back into bed together. She tells him it’s got to be the last time, though, because if John doesn’t leave town, he’s going to be killed. John says he can’t leave because he wants to find out why everyone is lying. That includes himself, Hal, Zoe, everyone. During the conversation, though, she also drops an interesting tidbit. Zoe says that she is the one who saved Macon, which goes up against his story. He said the Manhunter saved him and Zoe was the nurse. So, wait, could it be? Is she the Manhunter? Probably not. Zoe leaves the hotel and is zapped from the sky by giant lasers, blowing up her car. Hal flies up to grab the satellite and, with the help of the Sheriff, they figure out where it came from. This feels odd to John, though. It’s too easy. He thinks whoever blew up Zoe wanted to be caught and that they should approach with caution. Hal agrees and is impressed with John’s detective instincts. Time for yet another one of those long, dense conversations. The first was the one with Sinestro. Then between John and the Guardian. Then with Macon. Then Zoe. Just so many crucial conversations in this episode. This one happens on the drive to the person who made the satellite, whom they believe to be the Manhunter. Sparked by Zoe’s death, Hal tells John that losing people is part of the job of Green Lantern. The best advice he can give him is to avoid all real relationships. The pair arrive at the address their detective work brought them to, which happens to be a high-tech slaughterhouse where we watch a cow get cut to pieces by lasers. Eventually, they find the man in charge, and he has one of the lasers focused on John’s parents’ house. If John and Hal kill him, John’s parents die too. This man hopes to prove he’s the Manhunter by revealing that he’s been watching them and plays the conversation John had with Laura Linney to Hal. Hal now knows that John was supposed to take the ring. But Hal is Hal. He kind of sidesteps that and traps the guy. He asks him a simple question that only he and the Manhunter would know: what color is Abin Sur? The man says he doesn’t remember, so Hal keeps pushing. He explains that Sinestro told him the only way to prove a Manhunter turned into a human is to kill them and take out their heart, which would be crystallized. Hal threatens to do exactly that, so the man relents and stops the countdown on John’s family. The man tells them the Manhunter is none other than Macon himself. The car ride home is more than a little tense (and, you guessed it, another one of the episode’s long, important conversations). Pretty much everything is now out in the open. Hal knows John has been talking to the Guardians and is set to take the ring. John just watched Hal almost get his parents killed. But they seem to get over it. John calls the aliens to let them know who the Manhunter is. And just when you thought that was it, Hal jabs at John again. He’s confused why John wasn’t upset that Zoe died. And he thinks it’s because John knows she isn’t dead. She’s the Manhunter. John agrees and tells Hal he didn’t mean to keep that from him. He just wasn’t sure. Hal doesn’t like the mistrust and proceeds to jump out of the car again, letting John smash into a phone pole. As the episode ended, something didn’t feel quite right. Every single conversation or scene in the episode was 100% clear, except that last one. John did react to Zoe’s death. And if he didn’t, it would have been perfectly in character not to do so. Hal’s suspicions and the reveal that Zoe is the Manhunter (presumably) just didn’t quite land as cleanly as everything else before it. Plus, can we trust it? Either way, it wasn’t the best end to an otherwise very eventful episode. What did you think of “The Weenie?” Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: Study Suggests AI-Generated Drug Could Slow Aging
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.82
An AI-generated drug showed early signs of potentially slowing aging, according to a new study out today in Nature Biotechnology, possibly taking the first small step towards using AI to cure all the diseases tech companies companies keep talking about. The new study centers on rentosertib, a drug from Insilico Medicine, an AI drug discovery and development company. From the onset, Insilico said it created rentosertib with the aim of both treating patients suffering chronic lung disease and extending their lifespan. In the study, the company showed that its drug managed to successfully reduce some of the biological markers of age, as measured by aging clocks, in a small set of patients. Aging clocks have moved from a sort of shorthand to a reference of where a person is in their life (“their biological clock is ticking”) to a real metric that aims to measure a person’s morbidity and mortality. A number of these clocks have been developed with AI to take many measurements—biomarkers in blood, physiological metrics, psychological assessments, etc.—and spit out a biological “age” meant to reflect a person’s overall health. In the 42 participants of the study, Insilico found that its drug managed to reduce their biological ages over the course of the 12-week trial, while those who received a placebo or no treatment saw their age increase or stay the same. The company used six different so-called aging clocks and noticed enough of a shift on all six to conclude that “the drug may modulate complementary dimensions of biological aging.” The idea of reducing aging certainly sounds good (and has become the obsession of some tech bro-types), but the actual utility of aging clocks is up for debate. There are several variations of these clocks, all of which take different approaches. The earliest versions, developed over a decade ago, track methylation, which observes chemical changes in DNA. More recent models focus on proteomics, or measuring blood proteins, which a 2024 study found could be used to determine if a person had a higher risk of age-related diseases. And while some researchers believe that these catch-all measurements could be useful, there’s still a long way to go before they become truly meaningful markers. Scientists have tried to kick-start the field and improve accuracy so that such tools can be used for research purposes, but there still isn’t a measurement that serves as a universally accepted “age” indicator—and some doctors have warned that leaning on these metrics could lead to pursuing the wrong interventions, seeking ways to slow aging indicators in a way that actually harms a body’s repair response. All that said, a pill that keeps a person’s body from succumbing to the effects of aging would be a breakthrough. Insilico’s pill is still a long way from being that—it’ll have lot of trials to go before getting any sort of regulatory approval.

item.title: In What Ways Are We Not Prepared for the Big One?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.75
The West Coast of the United States lies on the Pacific ring of fire, the most seismically active region in the world. It’s home to two major faults, the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia Subduction Zone in the Pacific Northwest, that are capable of producing catastrophic earthquakes. Both are long overdue for one. The last time a major quake struck the San Andreas was 120 years ago, and now scientists say stresses along this fault are the highest they’ve been in the last 1,000 years. The Cascadia Subduction Zone hasn’t produced one since 1700, when a magnitude 9 quake—one of the largest in recorded history—triggered a tsunami that decimated the coast of Japan. Scientists say it’s not a matter of if, but when, the next disaster strikes. Commonly called “the big one,” this hypothetical but inevitable quake could come at any time, so communities need to be ready. Recent events have served as tragic reminders of just how devastating these natural disasters can be. In June, a pair of earthquakes killed more than 6,500 people in Venezuela, and other large quakes in the Philippines, Indonesia, and Columbia have killed hundreds over the summer. For this Giz Asks, we asked experts what gaps remain in the West Coast’s preparedness. They highlight vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that could hinder recovery from a catastrophic earthquake and exacerbate its toll. The following responses may have been lightly edited for length and clarity. Yumei Wang Affiliate faculty and senior advisor on infrastructure resilience and risk at Portland State University’s Maseeh College of Engineering & Computer Science. Wang’s research focuses on the transformation of communities from vulnerability to resilience in the face of disasters, including Cascadia earthquakes and tsunamis. She also has extensive experience with post-earthquake investigations around the world. When children go to school, they should be in buildings that are reliably safe. When someone in need calls 911, they should reach help. Critical infrastructure is essential not only for normal societal functioning but also for public safety. However, much critical infrastructure remains vulnerable to extensive damage from earthquakes. As evidenced by recent earthquakes and numerous engineering risk studies, services provided by critical infrastructure after earthquakes are often severely compromised. Water services may be unavailable for months. To assure effective response and timely recovery after earthquakes, it is imperative that the reliability and resilience of critical infrastructure be substantially improved. Civic infrastructure—schools and emergency response facilities, such as hospitals and fire stations—are important community assets that serve as safety nets during emergencies. Lifeline systems—water, wastewater, electricity, natural gas, liquid fuels, communications, and transportation—provide basic societal services that are needed for earthquake response and recovery. The Pacific Northwest is threatened by a future megaquake on the Cascadia Subduction Zone. A magnitude 9 earthquake and tsunami would likely produce an unprecedented catastrophe. Citizens should expect a regionwide electrical blackout, widespread bridge losses impacting transportation mobility, prolonged gasoline shortages associated with damaged pipelines, extended natural gas service outages, damages exceeding $100 billion, and tens of thousands of casualties. In Oregon, we took an innovative approach to evaluate seismic safety deficiencies of schools and emergency response facilities and have statewide policies and grant programs to help mitigate deficiencies. Furthermore, Oregon has systematically identified and quantified expected post-earthquake delays in resumption of basic lifeline services, which are reflected in the Oregon Resilience Plan. Although many impressive efforts to strengthen lifeline systems have been and continue to be made, Oregon is only in its early stages of needed earthquake preparations. With the expected destruction, citizens are urged to prepare to be “on your own” for at least two weeks. Currently, significant vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure exist, particularly the reliability of lifeline services after earthquakes. Lifeline system interdependencies, lack of coordination among systems, and the absence of regulatory oversight on service deliveries underpin the lack of readiness in earthquake prone regions. To improve earthquake preparedness, society must make it a top priority to remedy the deficiencies in our critical infrastructure, especially within lifeline systems. Greg Beroza Wayne Loel Professor of Earth Science at Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability. Beroza’s research interest is in analyzing seismograms to understand how earthquakes work and to quantify the hazards they pose, and his group works to improve earthquake monitoring in all settings by applying data mining and machine learning techniques to large volumes of continuous seismic waveform data. It’s been 120 years since the last large urban earthquake in the U.S. (1906 San Francisco). Recent earthquakes in Türkiye and Venezuela, where the geology is not that different from California, offer a glimpse of what could be in store. I don’t think we’re prepared for what’s coming. The infrastructure of civilization—internet, cellular coverage, electricity, gas, water, sewage, hospitals, roads, railroads, bridges, ports—are all susceptible to earthquake damage. These are critical to effective post-earthquake response. Following the big one, the degree to which they are damaged will compromise response, so we need to harden them. Building codes will help protect us, but the earthquake-resistant provisions in them are similar to those in other countries. They are also intended to ensure survivability of occupants, not the continuing viability of most buildings. If the occupants escape, but buildings are a total loss, that would be considered a success. That might not feel like success, and I don’t think we’re prepared for the economic fall out that would result from the concentrated loss of many buildings and infrastructure. There are secondary effects as well. A large earthquake in Cascadia would generate a tsunami that would compound the damage by striking the coast soon after the earthquake. A large earthquake in California would rupture gas lines and start fires at dozens of widely dispersed points. Fighting those fires would be difficult because communications, water supply, and transportation would all be impacted. This happened in 1906 when fires started, merged, and raged for three days, burning most of San Francisco to the ground. If an earthquake strikes during a period of high winds, it’s difficult to comprehend what might follow. Earthquakes and their effects are inevitable and pose an acute threat. They are rare, fortunately, but that rarity makes them difficult to study. It also makes them tempting to ignore relative to more commonly encountered threats. Their onset is sudden, however, so we need to act now to understand them and to build structures, cities, and systems to withstand them. Once the big one begins it will be too late. Jonathan Stewart The Sabol-Scott Term Chair in Civil and Environmental Engineering and a professor of civil and environmental engineering at UCLA’s Samueli School of Engineering. Stewart’s research interests are in geotechnical earthquake engineering and engineering seismology. His group works to learn from past earthquakes to improve understanding of seismic events and apply that understanding to the development of practical models. Let’s begin by reviewing positive developments. Since the 1994 Northridge earthquake, the California Department of Transportation has made significant advances in how to effectively retrofit bridges and has implemented those improvements. State legislation has mandated seismic assessments of hospitals, which has led to many retrofits and some hospital structure replacements. Mandatory retrofit ordinances have been implemented in some municipalities, including Los Angeles and San Francisco. We should celebrate these advancements.While progress has been made, California continues to face substantial earthquake risk, which is influenced by our location on a plate boundary but is also affected by the political will to confront vulnerabilities. Urban centers receive essential fresh water from aqueducts that cross major faults. For example, in Los Angeles, we receive more than half our water from three systems (Los Angeles Aqueduct, California Water Project, Colorado River Aqueduct), which cross the San Andreas Fault and could be ruptured by a single earthquake. Emergency reservoirs west of the fault are in place but are a temporary fix. We will be in a race against time to repair the aqueducts as the emergency reservoirs are depleted. Will this occur fast enough? Even if regional water supply is intact, breaks in water distribution systems and sewer systems from ground failure (i.e., liquefaction and landslides) are likely to lower water pressures, potentially rendering delivered water as non-potable. This will significantly impact daily life for earthquake survivors. While relatively modern, code-designed structures in strongly shaken areas are likely to survive the earthquake, some may be damaged to an extent that re-occupancy is not possible. This will lead to significant household and business displacement, potentially leading to de-population and impacting local economies. Whether that impact is short-term or long-term will depend on the pace of recovery, which is uncertain. Some structures, mainly older vulnerable buildings that have not been retrofitted, will collapse, costing lives. It is a tragedy waiting to happen. The severity of these impacts will depend on earthquake location relative to the locations of vulnerable buildings. Giz Asks is a recurring Gizmodo series in which experts answer big questions in their own words, offering a range of perspectives on the ideas, discoveries, and debates that affect our lives and shape our understanding of the world.

item.title: You don’t need to code or spend money to improve KDE—here are 7 ways to help
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.85
Open-source software is wonderful: it's free, diverse, and surprisingly accessible. You might feel that software development is a secret world of privilege and insider knowledge, but OSS has made great strides to overturn this misunderstanding. Whatever your skill set, you can make a difference and improve open-source software like KDE. If you can write, draw, code, speak more than one language, or just use your system, you can help out. Use KDE as much as possible By running the desktop, you're helping out without even realizing it OK, this might sound too good to be true, but just by using KDE, you are helping to improve the overall system: congratulations! First, the built-in Dr Konqi software will automatically offer to send a bug report if a KDE app ever crashes. This contains details of what happened and your current environment, so the devs can debug the problem. You don't have to report bugs, but it just takes a single button press to do, so there's little reason not to. You can also report telemetry data by enabling it in KDE's System Settings app, via the User Feedback module. This sends anonymous information about the apps you run, how long you run them for, and so on. Again, this is entirely optional, but it's vital for the system to improve based on real-world usage. Report any bugs manually A well-crafted bug report is invaluable to the developer team If you encounter a more complex crash, like a bug in an app that doesn't support Dr Konqi, you can report it manually using the KDE Bugzilla issue tracker. This process isn't for the faint-hearted, but you can rest assured that your feedback will help to improve the system for everyone. The bug tracker isn't the only way to report something; you can send ideas, discuss new features, or alert the developers to security vulnerabilities too. Flex your design skills With your help, KDE can look its very best Let's face it: engineers aren't always the best qualified when it comes to creating stunning imagery, or even designing slick interfaces. Linux has long suffered from a perception that it just doesn't look that good, and while this complaint is a bit overplayed, there's an element of truth to it. Fortunately, you can help, either by working on the look of the core product or on a secondary element like a KDE project's web design. Even more fortunately, all the tools you'll need are freely available, from KolourPaint-a quick and simple paint tool-to GIMP, the free alternative to Photoshop that's packed full of features. The KDE team uses familiar tools like Figma for collaboration, and you can contribute icons, cursors, wallpapers, and many other types of artwork. Translate text Help people all around the world KDE software is used worldwide, with around 60–80 different languages supported depending on the component. All those languages need translators to convert in-app text and documentation. If you're suitably qualified, check out the KDE Localization team, which deals with language translation alongside other international issues; everything from icon design to text encoding. Work is organized using mailing lists; there will either be one for the application you're interested in, or you can use the general-purpose kde-i18n-doc Write documentation Explain how things work and help others understand the system If you only know one language, that's fine; there's still plenty of writing to be done! Another task that developers often fail at — or are simply uninterested in — is writing documentation. If you have a flair for prose, consider the many areas in which your words can be a part of KDE. Most end-user documentation is hosted online at the many wikis maintained by the project. Again, the central point of contact — and best place to begin — is a mailing list, kde-doc-english. Spread the word Tell everyone else how amazing a free OS can be Are you an expert in marketing or a social media pro? If so, KDE can use your talents in promotion. Members of the KDE Promo team reach out to existing and potential users to discuss what the desktop does and how it can help them. The promotion effort takes in a variety of activities, from writing blog posts to attending conferences and scouting for new contributors. If you're a people person, this is certainly a great way to get involved. Make code contributions Build the apps, libraries, and core utilities that define KDE Last — but far from least, of course — is the work involved in building KDE, the software itself: programming. You'll start by learning to build KDE and its associated programs, using a freely available toolset. There's more information in the official mailing list, kde-devel, and you can even join a mentoring scheme for one-to-one assistance with an experienced developer. Remember that you can use a developer skill set for more than just hardcore programming, too: bug triaging, software testing, and technical documentation all benefit from knowledge and understanding of the codebase. Contributing can be addictive, even in small quantities I've personally contributed to open-source software, but only in fairly small ways: a bug report here, a minor patch there. But every time I've had code accepted into a project, it's accompanied by a warm, fuzzy feeling that my work has been appreciated and is genuinely going to help other people too. But there are many ways you can contribute to open-source projects, even without coding, and there's plenty more information on contributing to KDE on the project's main Get Involved page.

item.title: I’ve programmed in VS Code for years and I’d recommend these shortcuts to every beginner
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.19
VS Code is a big deal. In Stack Overflow’s 2025 Developer Survey, a whopping 76% of respondents said they use it regularly.
