That towers over the 29% who report using its nearest competitor, Visual Studio. If you’re new to VS Code, it can be a bit overwhelming at first. Remember, though, this is an IDE, a much more complex tool than a standard text editor. By easing yourself in with a few simple keyboard shortcuts, you can learn the basics without too much effort. Open the command palette Use Ctrl + Shift + P for instant access to thousands of commands If you can only remember one keyboard shortcut, make it this one. The command palette hosts a huge number of commands, tailored to your current context. Start typing, and the list will filter down to a much more manageable set. You can use this to find forgotten commands, discover new ones, or simply save time if you haven’t got the right shortcut to hand. Unless stated, all shortcuts presented here work the same on macOS, with Cmd substituted for Ctrl. The concept of a command palette is fast becoming a standard, as is this specific keyboard shortcut to access it. Some of VS Code’s competitors, like Zed, have adopted it, meaning it’s a great one to commit to memory. View keyboard shortcuts Use Ctrl + K, Ctrl + S to jog your memory Let’s face it, you’ll never remember all the many keyboard shortcuts, and nor do you need to. With a simple two-step shortcut, you can pull up an enormous list of every command that’s available, along with its keyboard shortcut, if any. Ctrl + K means hold down the Ctrl key and press K. Ctrl + K Ctrl + S means do the same, then follow it by holding down Ctrl and pressing S. You can keep the Ctrl key held down or release it between pressing the others; it’s up to you. Fortunately, you can filter this list too, so type in any part of a command to narrow down the choice. You can even search for the name of a key, including special ones like Ctrl or Backspace, to list commands with a shortcut that involves it. Open any file in your project Use Ctrl + P to search for files and open them VS Code’s explorer panel shows a tree-based view of all the files in your current project. It’s a great way to navigate using the mouse, but it’s not so accessible with the keyboard — unless you set up your own shortcuts to access it, at least. While you can press Ctrl + O to bring up the standard file open dialog, a better way to open a file is by pressing Ctrl + P to summon the Quick Open palette. This contains a fuzzy-searchable set of your project files, minus any that are system files or dependencies, like .git/ or node_modules/. This list is also sorted with the most recently opened files at the top, so it’s very useful for navigating quickly back and forth among a small set. Jump to definition Use F12 to see how (and where) a function, variable, or class is defined Getting a bit less meta now, this shortcut really showcases VS Code’s central selling point as an IDE that helps you code more efficiently. With a thorough understanding of your files at a syntax level, VS Code can assist you in ways far beyond that of a standard text editor. One of the most valuable and easy to understand is the humble F12 shortcut, for “Go to Definition.” As if by magic, this shortcut will transport you from any mention of a variable, function, or class to its corresponding definition. Start with your cursor anywhere inside a name, then, press F12, and VS Code will switch to that symbol’s definition, opening its file if necessary: Fold or unfold a region Use Ctrl + Shift + [ or ] to focus on different parts of your codebase Another advantage of VS Code’s language awareness is its support for region folding. If you’re navigating large or complex code files, it can help to zone in on one function or class definition at a time by temporarily collapsing others. If you’re deprecating a function, it can be easier to fold it than comment it out or delete it altogether. On macOS, the equivalent shortcuts are Cmd + Alt + [ and Cmd+Alt+]. There are also shortcuts to fold and unfold all regions, so — with practice — you can quickly minimize distractions and focus on just the code that needs your current attention. Toggle the terminal panel Use Ctrl + ` to access a command line without leaving your editor Another great benefit that most IDE’s introduce beyond standard text editors is an integrated terminal. Many programming projects will require you to drop into a command line from time to time, for the occasions when even VS Code’s toolbox is left wanting. To open the terminal panel at any time, simply press Ctrl + `. You’ll have a full command line at your disposal, using your familiar shell and environment. The current working directory will be set to your project directory, and you can even have separate tabs and split terminals. When you’re done, just tap Ctrl + ` again to return to the file you were editing. This shortcut is a rare case that’s identical on macOS, using Ctrl, not Cmd. Just a tiny fraction of shortcuts reveal VS Code’s power These keyboard shortcuts are essential, and you’ll do well to pick them up as early as possible, once you start using VS Code. There are many other very useful, but more advanced shortcuts, like moving a line using Alt + Up/Down. You can also copy or cut a whole line by pressing the standard Ctrl+C/X with no text selected. For a full reference, consult the keyboard shortcut PDFs for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

item.title: 3 long-dead programming languages that can still land you a good job
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.94
The programming world isn't just about Rust or TypeScript, and huge swaths of the economy rely on systems and technologies we rarely think about. These represent an opportunity, and dying languages that carry a lot of weight may offer the best of them. If niche technologies spark your interest, then this one's for you. A legacy language is one that was left behind. However, in reality, such languages never really go away. COBOL was invented in an era when smoking cigarettes was considered perfectly healthy, yet it still underpins most of the world's finances. Learning one means picking up tools that others have long forgotten about, sometimes giving you a distinct advantage, and earning staying power in fields that desperately need your skills. Here are three programming languages that could make you invaluable to certain employers. Common Business-Oriented Language (COBOL) ~$100k salary to maintain legacy code COBOL was one of the earliest high-level languages ever conceived, appearing in 1960—almost a full decade before we landed a tin can on the moon. Its initial purpose was to keep ordinary stakeholders (like managers) in the loop with complex business processes by using plain old English as its syntax. Since then, it has transformed into a behemoth, working its way into the heart of nearly every business transaction on Earth. Today, it's thought to handle a significant portion of the world's business and financial processes, such as 95% of ATM transactions and 40% of online-banking systems. The US government still relies on COBOL heavily across the board, not least the IRS. COBOL primarily runs on mainframe computers, where it crunches numbers and batch-processes data for a variety of industries. However, most code is in maintenance mode, and organizations are likely to phase it out over the next… say… 500 years. Franklin University reports the median salary of COBOL developers at around $99k, with the top of that range, roughly $167k, reserved for expertise in the finance industry. So, if you're looking to break into the financial sector and have an encyclopedic knowledge of proprietary financial systems, you can find a list of companies that rely on COBOL via TheirStack. Ada: For high-assurance applications ~$86k salary, and a resurgence in popularity in 2025 Ada (named after Ada Lovelace) first appeared in the early 80s as a project of the DoD. The intent was to replace the litany of programming languages it used at the time. It targets embedded and real-time systems where high assurance is critical, like avionics, air traffic control, transportation, military, and space technologies. Famous examples include the Boeing 777, F-22 Raptor, Eurofighter Typhoon, and satellites. The language has a strong focus on code correctness and a proven ecosystem in safety-critical industries, which is why it has survived as long as it has. One of Ada's primary features is its first-class support for design-by-contract (DbC): essentially preconditions, postconditions, and invariants that create strong guarantees on program state. Ada also provides built-in constraint checks, which catch memory access violations, range errors, and off-by-one errors at runtime. In addition to those, it has a strong type system and provides low-level access. The DoD dropped its Ada mandate sometime during the 90s, and outside its established moat, the language sort of just faded away. However, given recent incentives to adopt and use memory-safe languages, Ada attracted significant interest in 2025, moving it into a top-ten spot in the TIOBE Programming Community Index, ahead of popular choices like Rust and TypeScript. I am personally fascinated by design-by-contract, and it's a brilliant way to ensure the utmost code correctness while reducing the size and complexity of a test suite. Landing an Ada job will earn you an average salary between $86k and $113k, depending on experience, according to PayScale. Perl: The glue code of the early web ~$106k salary, but its days are numbered Perl debuted in 1987 as a general-purpose Unix scripting language, and it is well regarded for its flexibility. Its primary strengths are string processing and pattern matching, which proved so favorable that it influenced the powerful Perl Compatible Regular Expressions (PCRE) library that's still in wide use today. A large part of Perl's legacy lies in CGI scripts, which web servers run to perform various backend tasks. Perl's days are now numbered, and long gone is its heyday. However, legacy Perl code still persists in the modern era, and TheirStack lists 39,192 companies that mention it in their job postings. PayScale describes the average salary at around $106k, which isn't an insignificant amount. Rare technologies may mean better job security, but do more research Obviously, don't make career decisions based on my opinion, and do further research on the languages for yourself. COBOL is definitely important, but how easy is it to accumulate the financial-sector knowledge required to land a position? I also doubt learning Ada is something that will land you work on the F-22 Raptor, but the broader scope of high-assurance computing could certainly seed some interesting ideas. The programming landscape isn't all TypeScript, Rust, and Zig, and many industries are desperate for applicants with a particular set of skills. Knowing these, especially the unusual ones, may just provide strong job security that yet another JavaScript developer doesn't have. Or it may simply make you a better programmer.

item.title: Don't buy a used Raspberry Pi until you understand these 4 "gotchas"
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.32
Memory price hikes have pushed new Raspberry Pi prices up across the board and the secondhand market has started looking more appealing than it has in years. Unfortunately, while used Pis can be good deals, the market is also full of pitfalls that don't exist when you buy new. There are a handful of specific things you should double-check before you hand over your money, ranging from damage to conflated model information. None of them are always deal-breakers, but they're potential problems worth keeping an eye out for. Not all Pi generations are equal Double-check which board you're buying I often see Raspberry Pis listed on Facebook Marketplace just as a "Raspberry Pi," with no further information—I'm left zooming in on poorly lit photos to try and determine which model I'm looking at. They can look fairly similar, especially if you don't spend a lot of time with them. The model and RAM matter enormously. The Pi 1 and 2 are both 32-bit, single-core devices, and the Pi 3b barely keeps up against modern Pis. As a concrete example, the Pi Zero 2, which is the size of a stick of gum, can get very close to the computational performance of a Raspberry Pi 3B, though the Zero 2 has only 512MB of RAM while the Pi 3B has 1GB. The Pi 1 and 2 are notably slower and not worth buying, unless you're just collecting them for fun. Software and OS support for older devices is going by the wayside as they've become outdated. Even if you can find software that'll run on them, the hardware spaces are now "bad" enough that you can't do that much with them anyway. Make sure you get a good look at the board and verify the specific model, RAM amount, and revision number against your needs. Watch for weird pricing fluctuations Scam prices are a bigger problem now Besides increasing the prices of Raspberry Pis to unprecedented heights, the memory crisis has also opened up a new scam avenue: fake price hikes. It is an unfortunate reality today that the price of computers and computer components often jump by $50, $100, or even more literally overnight. Scammers have started taking advantage of that and deliberately hiking prices above even the inflated "true" retail price to make a buck, hoping that the unwary buyer pays without double-checking the pricing. Amazon third-party sellers and Facebook Marketplace resellers seem to have been the worst offenders, and I'd be careful buying any PC component or SBC from one. Raspberry Pi deliberately rolled out lower-memory options to help keep costs manageable. If you do need a Pi, I'd get it from one of the Raspberry Pi Foundation's approved vendors if possible. If you do buy a Pi used, double-check the current market price from one of those vendors, not Amazon. Run it before you buy it GPIO pins, ports, and power circuitry can be subtly damaged Raspberry Pis aren't like GPUs. They live fairly difficult lives as computers go—they get dropped, attached to drones and flown into trees, people carelessly attach power supplies to GPIO pins, or spend 18 months outside in an allegedly-waterproof box. That also means that used Pis often have pretty significant wear and tear. Before you buy a Pi, power it on and make sure it at least starts. Some damage (like a bent or broken GPIO pin) is readily repairable; a cooked memory module is a different class of problem entirely. If you see signs of burn marks or large amounts of flux residue (a sign someone has been soldering, which can damage components), I'd stay clear completely. Check for counterfeits, clones, or stripped boards I've seen too many fakes There aren't too many counterfeit Raspberry Pis out there on the used market, but it is very common to see other SBCs mislabeled as something like a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It has also been fairly common historically for a seller to use a picture of a Raspberry Pi and then hand you a clone, like an Orange Pi. There is nothing inherently wrong with the clones. Some of them are great, but if you're paying for a Pi, you should get a Pi. Clones also often lack the same software support Pis have, which can be a huge headache. I've also noticed that an increasing number of SBCs are sold on Facebook Marketplace with their RAM removed, presumably so someone can either sell the RAM separately for a premium or use it in a project of some kind. Sometimes this is surreptitiously mentioned in the listing; other times you'll just notice that there is a weird empty spot on the board in a photo. Whatever the seller's motivation and honesty level is, a Pi without RAM is useless—don't buy one. Don't trust a deal that seems too good to be true To buy a Pi safely, always double-check the specific model, double-check the price, and make sure to look for signs that it is physically damaged. If you take those precautions, you can actually find some pretty good deals still. Many people that purchased Pi 5s at release are willing to let their old, used Pi 4 go at a very reasonable price. The Pi 4 is a bit older now, but fully capable of hosting a small media server, a Pi Hole, or running any number of other small homelab jobs. I would generally recommend against buying the Pi 5 1GB or 2GB variants used; they still sell for "reasonable" prices compared to their higher-memory variants, and the trouble that comes with used SBCs is not worth the small savings you might get on a current-gen device.

item.title: You probably bought the wrong NFC tags for your smart home projects
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.04
NFC tags can be incredibly useful smart home tools. They're cheap to buy, and you can use them to trigger automations just by scanning them with a phone. Not all NFC tags are created equal, and it's all too easy to buy the wrong NFC tags for the job. Standard NFC tags may not work on metal Sticking tags to appliances can cause issues This was something I discovered when I first stuck an NFC tag to the side of a washing machine. I wanted to scan the tag to start an automation that would alert me when the washing cycle was finished, but I was struggling to get the tag to scan. I went through a few NFC stickers, assuming that I had a faulty batch. It turned out that it wasn't the fault of the NFC tags at all. The problem was that I was sticking them to the metal casing of the washing machine. NFC tags communicate using a magnetic field, and attaching the tag to conductive metal can interfere with that field. It means that the effective distance that you can scan the tag from is significantly reduced, making it much harder to scan the tag than normal. There are two solutions to this problem. The first is to stick the tag to a non-metallic part of the device. This isn't always possible if you want to attach tags to something that's predominantly made of conductive metal. In these cases, you can opt to use anti-metal NFC tags. These tags have a layer of shielding material behind the tag so that the antenna isn't stuck directly to the metal surface. An anti-metal tag should work far better on a metal surface than a standard NFC tag. Smaller tags come with a trade-off They're easier to hide but harder to use When you buy NFC tags, it's tempting to go for the smallest size you can find. One of the benefits of NFC tags is that they're easy to hide away, unlike bulkier smart buttons. I have NFC tags under plant pots, stuck to the side of my bed, and on the dashboard of my car. The problem with opting for smaller NFC tags is that while the chip itself can be tiny, it needs an antenna surrounding it for the tag to work. The smaller the NFC tag, the less space there is for the antenna. This means that a larger NFC tag can usually be more forgiving than a smaller one. If you opt for a tiny tag, you may need to be quite accurate about where you place your phone to scan the tag. With a larger tag that has a bigger antenna, the effective scanning distance can be greater, making it easier to scan the tag without having to be so precise. This is particularly useful if you've placed an NFC tag in a location that's awkward to reach, such as under a table. A larger tag can make it easier to scan the tag without having to hit the same exact location every time. Don't pay for storage that you don't need You're probably not going to need more than 144 bytes If you're buying NFC tags, you may see identifiers such as NTAG213, NTAG215, and NTAG216 in the product names. These identifiers refer to different NFC chip models that offer different amounts of available user memory. NTAG213 gives 144 bytes of user memory, NTAG215 has 504 bytes, and NTAG216 provides 888 bytes. It's easy to assume that getting NTAG216 tags makes the most sense, since it gives you the most user memory to play with. The reality is that for most smart home applications, even 888 bytes is overkill. The NFC tag is often used solely as a trigger for automations, with any necessary data for those automations coming from other sources. The NFC tag only needs to store a small amount of information, such as the short URL that Home Assistant uses to identify the tag. The 144 bytes offered by NTAG213 tags are more than enough to contain the information necessary for an NFC tag to work as a Home Assistant trigger, for example. You can buy an NTAG216 tag, but all that extra user memory will simply be going to waste. Even if you want to use a tag to store information, such as Wi-Fi credentials, an NTAG213 tag is usually enough, provided that the credentials aren't excessively long. Higher capacity NFC tags can often cost more than NTAG213 tags, so in the vast majority of cases, you'll just be wasting money. Stickers aren't the only option Different formats can work better for some uses Stickers are one of the most popular forms of NFC tags because they're incredibly easy to use. You can slap a sticker on most surfaces, making it easy to hide away discreetly. Stickers aren't the only option, however. NFC chips and antennas are sold inside cards, key fobs, wristbands, plastic tokens, and more. You can even use household objects. For some uses, these different formats can be more useful than stickers. For example, you could use an NFC key fob to trigger an automation that shares your location when you're driving somewhere. NFC cards are a popular choice for making NFC movie libraries that play different movies depending on which tags are scanned. The more solid options, such as discs or cards, are much better when you want to move the tags around rather than fix them in a single location. Sticking NFC stickers to things such as cards or other objects can work, but stickers can be more vulnerable to damage from bending or repeated handling, so other formats may still be a better option. NFC tags are useful as long as you choose wisely For many use cases, standard NFC stickers will do the job just fine. There are lots of situations where these aren't always the best choice, so you should think about what you want them to do before pulling the trigger on that pack of 200 stickers.

item.title: I ditched Google Keep and replaced it with a notes app that actually respects my privacy
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.61
Google Keep is convenient, but convenience came with a cost many people would want to stop paying: my notes living in Google's cloud, tied to my account, scanned by whatever systems Google runs behind the scenes. Switching to Obsidian changed how I think about my own notes entirely. What is Obsidian? A local-first app built on plain markdown files Obsidian is a note-taking app that stores everything as plain markdown text files on your own device rather than in a proprietary database sitting on someone else's server. When you open the app for the first time, you create what Obsidian calls a vault, which is really just a folder on your storage. Every note you write becomes an individual .md file inside that folder, readable by any text editor on any operating system, with or without Obsidian installed. It doesn't really get any simpler. This design choice is the foundation of everything else the app does well. Because notes are stored locally by default, Obsidian works fully offline, and there is no account required to use it. The app itself is free even for work use, and that free version includes the full editor, unlimited vaults, and every core feature rather than a stripped-down trial. What matters the most for me, compared to other alternatives, is its linking system. Notes can reference one another using double bracket syntax, and Obsidian visualizes those connections in a graph view that shows how your ideas relate to each other over time. This is often described as a form of networked or Zettelkasten-style note-taking, where the value comes not just from individual notes but from the web of links between them. Beyond that, the app supports an enormous plugin ecosystem, letting people extend it with everything from spaced-repetition flashcards to Kanban boards to calendar integrations, all built by the community rather than the company itself. Why is it better? Ownership and privacy replace convenience as the priority The clearest advantage Obsidian has over Google Keep is who controls the data. With Keep, your notes live on Google's servers, subject to Google's terms of service, retention policies, and whatever automated systems process account data across its products. With Obsidian, notes sit in a folder you own, in a format that will still be readable decades from now, regardless of whether the company behind the app exists. There is no ad tracking built into the core experience, no requirement to sign in, and nothing about the note-taking process that touches a server unless you deliberately choose to enable one. That last point matters because Obsidian does not force offline use. If multi-device access matters to you, the company sells an optional sync service, and that syncing is end-to-end encrypted, meaning even the Obsidian team cannot read the contents of synced notes. That is a meaningfully different privacy posture than a note living unencrypted in a cloud account tied to your broader Google profile. The plugin system reinforces this sense of ownership. Rather than waiting on a single company's product roadmap for new features, the community builds and maintains extensions, and users choose exactly which ones to install. Nothing is forced into the base app that you have not opted into. Combined with the plain markdown format, this means switching away from Obsidian later, should you ever want to, involves no export process or data migration headache. The files were always yours in a format every other editor understands, which is the opposite of how most note apps, Keep included, are designed to work. Should I use it? It depends on how much you value control over convenience Obsidian is worth adopting if privacy and data ownership matter more to you than having a note app that syncs instantly and invisibly the moment you install it. Anyone coming from a simple, disposable note-taking habit, jotting down grocery lists or quick reminders, will likely find Obsidian's learning curve unnecessary. Keep, or a similar lightweight app, still does that job fine. Where Obsidian earns its place is with people building something more permanent: research notes, project documentation, journaling, or a long-term personal knowledge base that benefits from linking ideas together over months or years. The tradeoffs are worth naming honestly. The free core app covers writing, linking, and organizing notes, but multi-device sync is not free. Obsidian Sync costs four dollars per user per month when billed annually, or you can avoid that fee entirely by syncing your vault folder through a service like iCloud, Dropbox, or a private Git repository, though those workarounds lack the official sync tool's built-in encryption and can be fiddlier on mobile. It is also worth mentioning that Obsidian is built for individual use rather than collaboration. There is no real-time multi-user editing the way Google Docs or even Keep's shared lists allow, so teams needing shared, simultaneously-edited notes will hit friction fast. A privacy-first note app worth the learning curve Obsidian trades Google Keep's instant convenience for something more durable: notes you fully own, stored locally, and encrypted if you choose to sync them. For anyone tired of their notes living on someone else's server, that tradeoff is an easy one.

item.title: 3 Home Assistant projects to repurpose old hardware this weekend (Sep 4-6)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.38
Tech prices are going through the roof, with the high cost of RAM affecting everything from Raspberry Pis to high-end gaming PCs. The good news is that with Home Assistant, it’s often possible to repurpose old tech so that you don’t need to buy anything new. Turn an old Echo Dot into a local smart speaker Escape the Alexa ecosystem When Alexa first appeared on the scene, it seemed like this might be the way that we would control all of our smart home devices. Shows such as Star Trek: The Next Generation made the idea of talking to our computers feel like the most efficient way to use them. The reality turned out to be disappointing. While Alexa is useful for basic things such as turning on lights or asking simple questions, Amazon’s locked-down ecosystem means that an Echo smart speaker today isn’t much more useful than it was when the first models launched. It’s a shame, because the hardware even in older Echo smart speakers is actually pretty solid, with microphone arrays and beamforming that can pick up voice commands even in noisy environments. Thankfully, if you have an old second-generation Echo Dot, you can break free of the shackles of Alexa and turn it into your own local smart speaker. There are several projects that let you use your Echo Dot as a local voice satellite for Home Assistant so that you can speak to Assist using your Echo without having your commands end up on Amazon’s servers. One project even allows you to run speech recognition and a small LLM directly on the device, so that much of the processing happens on the Echo rather than on your Home Assistant server. Whichever option you choose, you can do a lot more by using an Echo Dot with Home Assistant than you ever could with Alexa. Build a smart home hub from a laptop motherboard The scale model of your home is optional There are plenty of options for running Home Assistant. I ran it for a couple of years on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ without any major issues, and I now run it in Proxmox on a mini PC. There are plenty of other suggestions that are often given, including running Home Assistant on an old laptop. The problem with using an old laptop is that you have to deal with issues such as maintaining battery health, high-power consumption, a mostly redundant screen, and the fact that it looks like an old laptop. One clever Home Assistant user solved this problem by ripping the motherboard out of an old laptop and running Home Assistant on it, using the laptop’s original cooling hardware along with the RAM and storage. A bare motherboard still isn't the most beautiful-looking Home Assistant server, so the user built an entire scale model of their home to house the motherboard and components. The model isn’t just for looks; it includes LEDs in the rooms to mimic the real lighting states, and an ESP32-S3 running ESPHome allows the user to talk to the house and get voice assistant responses. You don’t have to go to the same extreme of building a tiny version of your own home. However, the idea of using the components from the laptop rather than the entire laptop itself is an interesting one and might be something worth considering if you have an old computer lying around. Give a Meta Portal a second life with Home Assistant Put abandoned hardware to good use There are plenty of tech devices that have come and gone without making much of an impact, and the Meta Portal (originally the Facebook Portal) is definitely one of them. Launched in 2018, the Portal was a line of smart displays primarily intended for video calling via Messenger or WhatsApp. By 2022, Meta ended development and sold off the remaining inventory of Portal products. For a long time, these devices were basically e-waste, but in June 2026, Meta added official Android Debug Bridge (ADB) support to the devices, allowing people to bypass many of the limitations of the locked-down Meta software and sideload their own Android apps. The upshot is that it’s now possible to do a lot with a Meta Portal. One community project uses Ava Pro, an Android platform built for Home Assistant, to turn the Meta Portal into a voice-controlled speaker for Music Assistant. Another option is Portal HA Bridge, which turns a Meta Portal into a Home Assistant device exposing screen controls, motion detection, camera streaming and more. As a result, some Home Assistant users are picking up old Portals from secondhand marketplaces. You can still find them for reasonable prices, but you might want to grab one before they become too scarce. Repurposing is one of the best things about Home Assistant I love Home Assistant for so many reasons, but the fact that you can often use it to repurpose old hardware is definitely up there. I’ve given new life to broken iPads, Echo Show devices, and old phones, saving me from having to buy new hardware.

item.title: 3 open-source virtual desktop tools that make Windows’s built-in feature look outdated
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.20
Windows 11 has a robust virtual desktop feature, but it is rather basic. It probably doesn't help that Microsoft only built its own virtual desktop solution long after Linux and macOS had shown us what they could do. The result is that there have been third-party virtual desktop apps for a long time now, across several versions of Windows. With so much time, user feedback, and competition, some of these third-party options are still going to be a better fit than the basic solution that comes with Windows today. There are quite a few options, but this is a good cross-section of what's out there. Desk Switcheroo puts a desktop manager on your taskbar And it has a portable version too! Desk Switcheroo is probably the most comprehensive replacement for the Windows Task View tool on this list. You get a compact widget that can be anchored close to your taskbar, from where you can make the magic happen. The widget shows the current desktop number, a custom label, and you can even set it to show you the current desktop's position within the total desktop count. You can use the arrow buttons or mouse wheel to shift between desktops without opening Task View. If you click the widget, you get a full desktop list, letting you jump to a specific labeled desktop instantly, again without opening Task View. You can also quickly create, delete, rename, and reorder your desktops. You can also assign each desktop a color and wallpaper, temporarily preview another desktop, or display thumbnail previews when hovering over entries. Desktop Switcheroo also adds some useful new tricks to window management. For example, you can pin a window across all your desktops, which is useful if you have to use your calculator app on different desktops without opening multiple iterations of it. A rules engine can automatically send matching windows to specific desktops, while event hooks can run commands when desktop-related events occur. SylphyHornPlus adds the controls Microsoft forgot It hides itself well Downloading or installing SylphyHornPlus can trigger your antivirus. As far as I can tell, this is a false positive and is related to how the app listens for global hotkeys. However, ensure you download the app from its real page, or use the Winget command to install it. SylphyHornPlus is a great choice if you already like the vanilla Windows virtual desktop interface, but want to expand what it can do. Instead of replacing Task View, it adds shortcuts, notifications, gestures, and management tools around the native feature without altering them. With global hotkeys, you can just switch directly to a specific desktop instead of scrolling through them, or using Task View. You can also use the hot keys to move windows to other desktops, create or remove them, and change their order. You can set up a notification that reminds you of which desktop you're on, and can have its position and appearance customized. It's not just the keyboard controls that are better. The app supports mouse wheel and rocker gestures. So you can do a lot of the stuff you want using just the mouse, but without clicking through a bunch of menus. While SylphyHornPlus doesn't have any window setup saving powers that I could see, you can export and save your app settings. So if you reinstall Windows or use more than one machine, you can have your tweaked settings on hand all the time. FancyWM gives every desktop a self-organizing layout What's old is new again FancyWM is only partly open-source. The author has open-sourced core parts of the backend, but the application itself is not open-source as a whole. You can download and use it for free, and make an optional payment to support them. The only difference is that you'll get an occasional pop-up asking you to support the project. FancyWM (Fancy Window Manager) is more than just a virtual desktop tool for Windows. It's a full-fledged window manager that could make your life so much easier. It uses dynamic tiling to make the most of your screen real estate, which automatically makes it great if you have an ultra-wide monitor or if you're using a large 4K display. When you open your apps, FancyWM automatically tiles them in panels, instead of letting them overlap. This is actually something that old versions of Windows did, using window tiling as the default. So it's interesting to see it come back as a productivity hack. It supports horizontal, vertical, and stacked panels, and these can be nested to build more complicated layouts. Windows automatically resize as applications are opened, closed, or moved. One thing that makes FancyWM stand out from other tiling window managers is that there's no trick here with a proprietary hidden workspace. Instead, the app integrated with Windows' native virtual desktop technology. This app is highly keyboard-driven if you want it to be. Using only the keyboard, you can instantly jump to any desktop or send the currently active window to another desktop. Panel arrangements can also be maintained globally or separately for each monitor. This all adds up to a much more powerful and cohesive system than combining Windows Snap Layouts with Task View virtual desktops. While Snap can quickly arrange your open windows into a layout, it doesn't keep managing them. FancyWM adapts your window tiles in real time as you open and close them. So each desktop ends up staying organized no matter what you're doing. There's nothing actually wrong with Windows virtual desktops out of the box, but if you start relying on this feature as part of your workflow, you'll quickly run into limitations that these apps can help solve.

item.title: I split my Chrome browsing into separate profiles, and suddenly ads stopped following me everywhere
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.19
Most of you reading this probably use just one Google Chrome profile to do everything. So that means your banking, work, leisure, and all other activities happen using the same online identity. Clearly, this works, but is it ideal from a privacy perspective? Instead of lumping everything you do online into a single identity, you can use the Chrome profiles feature to keep things separate that should not mix. It's less hassle than using separate browsers! A new profile gives you a genuinely separate cookie jar Literal internet cookies, by the way Creating a profile is as easy as going to Settings -> [Your Name] -> Add new profile. Chrome profiles aren't just workspaces or a way to organize tabs. Each profile creates a completely separate storage space and identity. That means your cookies, browser history, saved passwords, and everything else are completely isolated from each other. You can choose to have each profile linked to an email address, which is going to be necessary if you want to use different Google Account for things like file storage or logging into websites. However, if you just want a separate profile for a purpose that does not require this, you can choose not to sign in and just use a local profile. This still keeps things separate, but that profile will not sync across devices. You can also create a "guest" profile, which is designed for those times when someone wants to use your computer to, for example, log into their bank account. When that profile is closed, it disappears. Of course, you can use the "Manage profiles" option located below the profile creation entry to remove any profiles you no longer need. Profiles stop one part of your online life spilling into another There's no reason Facebook needs to know about your action figure obsession Because profiles are kept this separate, it means that you can't be tracked across profiles and, as far as advertisers or other interested parties are concerned, you're two completely different users. For example, for my job, I have to research a ton of products on sites like Amazon and beyond. I also have to do research on topics that I don't want sites to track for use during my personal browsing. So, by having a separate work profile, I can prevent the ads I see during normal browsing from being completely bonkers. More importantly, perhaps, is that having multiple profiles makes it less likely that you'll upload a personal file to your work Google Drive, for example. It does help that Chrome windows from different profiles aren't the same color! Profiles allow you to log onto the same website in separate Chrome sessions, and that's also a good safety net. How many times have we seen social media managers accidentally make personal posts using a work account because they rely on a site like X to juggle those profiles? Having separate Chrome profiles reduces the odds of that happening significantly. Profiles let you quarantine extensions instead of trusting them everywhere If you must have them, separate them Perhaps the biggest boon from using Chrome profiles relates to extensions. Like most technology outlets, we've highlighted the dangers of Chrome extensions for decades and always recommend you either only use ones made by Google or otherwise minimize your use of extensions as much as possible. But, by using Chrome profiles, you can spread out your extensions. After all, most of the extensions you use are probably ones that don't need to be active all the time. If your extensions group into different use cases, you can create a Chrome profile for each. That way, if an extension turns out to be malicious, you limit what it can see and what damage it can do. Profiles are privacy compartments, not an invisibility cloak It's very important to understand that Chrome profiles only help protect your privacy in very specific ways. It's not a substitute for other forms of security like VPNs. Chrome profiles don't make you anonymous; they just give you several identifications. Each of which can still be traced back to you. Some tracking methods are at a level above Chrome profiles. Your IP address is still the same regardless of profile. Unless you use something like a VPN as well. Likewise, information about your computer such as its specs, operating system, or the hardware level ID of your network device are still exposed. You'd have to run Chrome from inside a virtual machine to get around that, as one example. Obviously, if you log into the same account across multiple profiles, the site provider will know those profiles are associated with one another. So there are numerous ways in which you can deliberately or confidentially nullify the benefits of compartmentalization. That said, Chrome's ability to manage multiple profiles is an incredibly powerful tool that can help you reduce some of the tracking and chaos that comes from working and living on the internet. So if you aren't already using this feature, it's time to create that disposable "research" profile at the very least.

item.title: 5 Google Messages features that make group chats far less chaotic
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.17
I have a lot of family and friends, which means I’ve somehow ended up in hundreds of group chats. There’s one for discussing common life problems, another for vacation planning, one for the family, and a few that I’m honestly not even sure why they were created. After a while, all these conversations become my digital junk drawer. But I don’t scroll through 200 messages just to find the restaurant name we decided on last week. Thankfully, Google Messages has a few clever features that help me keep things under control. These are the ones I use to keep my group chats from turning into complete mayhem. I turn group-chat chaos into a shared list Create and edit Google Keep notes without leaving the chat We all have one friend who is fond of traveling. I’ve got one too. He can turn a weekend plan into a 100-message group-chat marathon. One person suggests a hotel, another shares a snack list to carry, someone asks about fuel costs, and before I know it, the important details are buried somewhere between memes and all those “okay, got it” messages. But now, we have Google Keep integrated into our Google Messages. The new Google Keep integration can be accessed by tapping the + icon inside a group chat. From there, you can create a shared note or list and add it directly to your messy conversation. Every participant in the group can view it, make changes, add new items, or check things off. My mom and I have a group named “The Grocery Cartel,” where we keep a shared note of grocery items. Instead of asking “Did you buy tomatoes?” for the tenth time, she can simply check the list. I’m definitely using this for our next trip to Spain. Custom names and icons make all the difference I gave my group chat some personality After organizing the information, it’s time to organize the chat itself. With hundreds of conversations in Messages, I sometimes have to pause and figure out which group I’m opening, especially when several of them have the same people. That’s where custom names and icons come in handy. Google Messages lets me give my RCS group chats custom names and icons. Now I don’t have to worry about having five vacation-planning groups, with three of them having the same people. I can instantly tell which group I need without opening each one and going through all the messages. It’s a small feature, but I like having it in Google Messages too, just like WhatsApp. I mute the groups that never stop buzzing Silence a specific group chat for a chosen duration Overexcited people simply don’t know when to stop. My family group can go from completely silent to 50 messages in under 5 minutes, usually when I’m at work or about to sleep. To be honest, most of those messages are just “Good morning” and “Good night.” Instead of muting my weekend-getaway group and missing important details, I can mute just the noisy family group for a day. I can unmute it once I am back on Monday. Google Messages lets me snooze a specific conversation. I can touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, and choose a duration of one hour, eight hours, 24 hours, or always. I can choose how long I want my peace to last, and my notifications resume when the snooze period ends. It’s perfect for those groups that are useful but occasionally become a little too enthusiastic. @Mentions make it easier to get someone’s attention No more shouting into the chat It happens to me all the time: I need someone’s attention, but everyone else decides to reply first. On Instagram or WhatsApp group chats, I simply @ a specific friend when I need to grab their attention. Now I can do the same in Google Messages through RCS group chats. “Hey, can you answer this?” doesn’t always work when you’re in a busy group chat. I can just type @ followed by my friend’s name and ask him which drink he wants me to get for the trip. It makes it obvious who I’m talking to instead of making everyone wonder which drink I’m talking about. Even better, the mentioned person gets a notification, which can save me from sending a follow-up message. In a group conversation, a tiny @ can save a lot of back-and-forth. Leave unwanted group chats Sometimes, I just leave the chaos For RCS group chats, Google Messages lets me exit the conversation. So, when a group has outlived its purpose, I don’t have to keep muting it or watching new messages pile up. I can just leave and move on. I’ve been part of an event group chat that ended months ago, but all the other members were still active in the group except for me. So, I decided to declutter my inbox and make peace with it. You can do this with any group where you brainstorm ideas with your team, a temporary chat created to plan a Sunday outing, or a friend group you’re no longer part of. Sometimes, the easiest way to make a group chat less chaotic is to stop being a part of it. Less chaos, fewer headaches I’ve accepted that my group chats will never be quiet. But at least I have a few ways to keep things from getting completely out of hand. And now, my phone can handle the chaos without dragging me into every conversation. That’s a pretty good deal for me.

item.title: These are the first 4 Android settings I change after a factory reset
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.37
Have you ever noticed that the factory reset on any phone does only half the job? Yes, it’s true. So, I never immediately start downloading my apps or restoring everything from my backup once it boots up. Instead, I take a few minutes to go through the settings and make my phone feel like mine again. After all, a factory reset is supposed to give you a fresh phone; why bring back all the clutter and defaults you were trying to get rid of in the first place? Trust me, make these changes the next time you reset your Android phone, and your freshly reset phone will feel less “factory” and a lot more yours. My first move: ditch buttons Now I don’t tap, I swipe First things first, before I start changing any other settings on my phone, I always change the way I move around it. I’ve never been a fan of the three-button navigation bar, especially when I can swipe my way through Android instead. So the first setting I change after a factory reset is gesture navigation. With gesture navigation enabled, I can simply swipe up from the bottom of the screen to go Home instead of moving my thumb to find the Home button, then swipe up and hold to see my recent apps. When I’m reading my own article, I swipe inward from either edge of the screen to go back to the page I was on before. This comes in handy, especially when I’m holding my phone in one hand. Mastering the bottom-edge swipe is also useful for quickly jumping between recent apps when I’m multitasking. Once these gestures become muscle memory, stretching my thumb down to reach for a button every time I want to navigate around my phone starts to feel like unnecessary work. Give gestures a try, and I bet you’ll forget those three buttons ever existed. I make the back do more Two taps, one handy shortcut The next feature I jump into is the one that makes me wonder why Samsung didn't turn it on by default. It’s the famous Back-Tap action. On my Galaxy Z Fold 6, it turns the back of my phone into a tiny but convenient shortcut. I can double-tap the logo to take screenshots, something I probably do 100 times a day, and it’s much easier than juggling the phone to press the Power and Volume Down buttons. I can also assign a different action to a triple tap, such as opening an app or triggering another shortcut. Samsung offers this through the RegiStar module in Good Lock: I open Good Lock, install RegiStar, tap Back-tap action, turn it on, and then choose what I want the double-tap or triple-tap to do. I usually keep double-tap for screenshots because I use it constantly. But if screenshots aren’t your thing, assign the double-tap to something that you frequently do. Once you get used to having an invisible button for your everyday tasks, reaching through menus to perform them will feel unnecessarily slow and boring. I will stop letting my notifications disappear One tap before they’re gone Once I start my phone after a factory reset, I’m bombarded with notifications like there’s no tomorrow. They’re usually alerts about apps I’ve just installed, updates, emails, messages, and so on. When my notification panel starts filling up, I usually start swiping them away without thinking, not realizing that the important ones can easily get buried among all that noise. That’s why enabling Notification History is one of the first things everyone should do. It keeps a record of recently dismissed notifications, so I can go back and check whether I’ve accidentally missed my mom’s message or a work email from my editor. On most Android phones, I go to Settings -> Notifications -> Advanced settings -> Notification History and turn it on. I don’t have to rely on my memory or hope that the notification pops up again after I dismiss it in a hurry. It’s a tiny safety net, but now I don’t panic because I can retrace anything I’ve swiped away while I’m half asleep on a Sunday afternoon. I give myself more screen time 30 seconds are way too short sometimes A 30-second screen timeout is way too short, especially for me, since I’m constantly reading articles or following a recipe my husband sent me. The problem is that I don’t always touch my phone while I’m cooking, so the screen can turn off right when I need to check the next step. I’d rather give myself a few extra minutes than keep waking up my phone every time the screen goes dark. On my Galaxy, I head to Settings -> Display -> scroll down until you see "Screen timeout" and increase the duration to 10 minutes. If your husband isn’t a foodie, you can choose a shorter duration that works for you. There’s also another handy option called Keep screen on while viewing, which uses the front camera to detect when you’re looking at the screen and keeps it on even if you’re not touching your phone. I turn this on, too. Just keep in mind that this feature may not be available on every Galaxy model or software version. You’ll realize how useful these settings are when you don’t have them. A fresh reset, my way A factory reset gives me a clean slate, but I don’t want to stop there. I’d rather spend a few more minutes tweaking the settings I know I'll use every day. So, the next time you do a factory reset on your Android phone, don't rush to restore everything and call it done. Check these settings first, and your future self will thank you.

item.title: I didn’t expect Dell’s entry-level XPS 13 to feel this premium
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.36
I’ll admit, I’m not sure what I was expecting when I first opened up the box for the latest Dell XPS 13 laptop. However, I know for sure I wasn’t expecting to love this tiny laptop as much as I do. At $699, this could be the mid-range Windows laptop to beat in 2026. Dell XPS 13 (2026) - Operating System - Windows 11 Home or Pro - CPU - Up to Intel Core Ultra 7 355, 8 cores, up to 4.7GHz - GPU - Integrated Intel Graphics - RAM - Up to 32GB LPDDR5x, up to 9600 MT/s Dell's latest XPS 13 is its smallest XPS yet. Packing the Core 5 or Core Ultra 7 processors and up to 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM, this ultra-compact laptop is perfect for your day-to-day tasks. - Ultra-compact, premium design - Strong everyday performance - Comfortable typing experience - Great screen - Limited speaker bass - Not designed for higher-performance tasks like gaming or photo/video editing Price and Availability The Dell XPS 13 is available to purchase directly from Dell and Best Buy, coming in three models with pricing starting at $699. There's the version reviewed here with a Core 5, 8GB RAM, 512GB storage, another model with the same Core 5 CPU, 16GB RAM, and 512GB of storage, and then the highest end model with a Core Ultra 7 CPU, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. Specifications - Brand - Dell - Operating System - Windows 11 Home or Pro - CPU - Up to Intel Core Ultra 7 355, 8 cores, up to 4.7GHz - GPU - Integrated Intel Graphics - RAM - Up to 32GB LPDDR5x, up to 9600 MT/s - Storage - Up to 1TB PCIe NVMe SSD - Battery - 52Wh, 3-cell - Display (Size, Resolution) - 13.4 inches, 2560 × 1600, 30–120Hz - Camera - 1080p at 30fps with infrared Windows Hello camera - Speakers - Four speakers; 8W total peak output - Colors - Sky or Storm - Ports - 2× USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 on Core 5 models; 2× Thunderbolt 4 on Core Ultra models; both support DisplayPort and Power Delivery - Network - Intel Wi-Fi 7 BE213, 2×2 - Dimensions - 11.69 × 7.9 × 0.5 inches (W × D × H) - Weight - Starting at 2.2 pounds (1kg) - Model - XPS 13 DX13260 - Adaptor and Battery - 65W USB-C adapter; 52Wh battery - Card Reader - None - Keyboard - Backlit keyboard with dedicated Copilot key - Display type - Touchscreen LCD, 500 nits, InfinityEdge - Audio - Four speakers and dual-array microphones - Security - Windows Hello facial recognition The Dell XPS 13 is one of the smallest laptops I've ever used Though small in build, it's mighty in features I've used many laptops throughout the years, the Dell XPS line included. While it's been about a decade since I've used an XPS, the XPS 13 absolutely blew me away with its size. Given how many laptops I've used over the years, I've also used my fair share of small laptops. The smallest laptop I've ever used has to be the 11-inch MacBook Air, or the 12-inch MacBook — both of which it's been about a decade since I've used. Many manufacturers have aimed at packing bigger laptops into smaller form factors, but Dell went a different direction with the latest XPS 13. It still has a 13.4-inch screen, but the body is basically designed around the display's panel. There are hardly any bezels on this laptop, and there isn't a wasted inch anywhere that I can find. Dell did an absolutely fantastic job on the design here. While you might expect this small laptop to lack major features, that's actually quite the opposite. Dell managed to pack a 1080p30 webcam in the XPS 13, alongside an IR camera for Windows Hello. Dual microphones are also present for a decent audio setup, and that's just the beginning. On either side of the XPS 13, you'll find a USB-C port. On the entry-level model (which is what I'm reviewing here) both ports are USB 3.2 Gen 2 with DisplayPort support and Power Delivery. On the models with the Core Ultra processors, both ports are Thunderbolt 4 with DisplayPort 2.1 and Power Delivery. The speakers are decent, but the small body definitely doesn't leave a lot of room for big, boomy bass. I don't mind watching a YouTube video on it or playing some background music, but I definitely fire up my Bose QuietComfort headphones whenever I want to actually enjoy listening to something. I was also quite surprised by the keyboard. One of the most surprising things to me is the power button. While it looks like a normal key, it's much more difficult to press, which is actually really nice as it means I won't accidentally click it when reaching for the backspace or delete key. The overall layout of the keyboard is a bit cramped for my personal preference, but it's a small laptop, and Dell did a really good job with the keyboard layout overall. I recently took a trip to Boston for a press event and brought the XPS 13 along with me and it was a joy to write on during the trip. Dell also got the trackpad almost perfect. It's a fairly great trackpad, all things considered, but I really wish it would have been a force touch trackpad. As it is, there's no middle pivot like we used to see in trackpads years ago (and some mid-range laptops still have), which is very nice to see. I had no issues using the trackpad, and I think it's a solid part of this laptop overall. I was surprised to find Wi-Fi 7 in tow here, which actually makes a marked difference in wireless performance if you have a compatible router. My UniFi Dream Router 7 was sitting about 10 feet away from the XPS 13 while I was downloading some games on Steam and Xbox, and the XPS 13 was seeing download speeds of 750 to 800Mb/s, which is nearly maxing out my network’s Gigabit WAN connection. Mid-range specs don't mean mid-range performance I'm amazed at how far mobile processors have come My review unit from Dell for the XPS 13 is the base model, which is actually somewhat surprising. Often, a brand will send out at least the mid-range, or even the top-tier model to give a reviewer the best experience possible. But, Dell made the right choice here, I think, when sending out the entry-level model. I was absolutely surprised by the performance of this laptop. And, since it's the base model, whether you buy the very model I'm using or a better one, you'll see the same or better results as what I got. The Core 5 320 CPU is part of Intel's Series 3 Core processors. It's got six cores, and the laptop has 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM installed. While that might not seem like a lot, it actually is more than enough for most workflows. As seen in the benchmarks, this laptop isn't breaking any records for its performance. However, where I'm surprised is just how usable it is being an entry-level laptop. I still remember years ago, I avoided anything that didn't have at least an i7 in it. Laptop or desktop, an i7 was a must. These days, a Core 3 or Core 5 is actually more than usable. Dell proves that here. While I wouldn't buy the XPS 13 for gaming, it actually handled Forza Horizon 5 better than I expected. Other games, like No Man's Sky and Minecraft, also run halfway decent here — though Minecraft with no mods definitely runs the best out of the three. Overall, the performance didn’t leave me hanging anywhere. I wouldn’t necessarily buy the base model to do heavy photo or video editing, but it definitely has enough juice to handle normal computer tasks, like writing documents, working with spreadsheets, browsing the web, and other normal things. Dell gets the everyday experience right with the XPS 13 Out of all the laptops I've tested, this is the one I consistently reach for The thing that surprised me the most about the XPS 13 is simply how much I enjoyed using the laptop. Often, I’ll use a laptop for a review and then move onto the next system (or back to my primary computer). With the XPS 13, that’s not exactly the case. Of course, I’m still using my more powerful MacBook Pro for my video and photo editing, but the XPS 13 has simply been a joy to use, and I keep reaching for it for simple tasks like browsing the web or writing articles. The overall experience is just superb on the XPS 13, and I don’t say that lightly. If someone asked me to recommend a mid-range, compact Windows laptop for everyday use, the XPS 13 is the first laptop that would come to my mind. Should you buy the Dell XPS 13? I’ve kind of already given away the answer, but yes, I think you should buy the Dell XPS 13, so long as you make sure to temper your expectations some. The higher end models will most surely handle more demanding tasks like video or photo editing better than my entry-level model. However, if you just need a solid laptop to browse Facebook Marketplace, watch YouTube or Netflix, and read How-To Geek, then the XPS 13 is a fantastic choice. At its $699 starting price, I really don’t think there’s another laptop in this price range that offers as premium of an experience as this one does. Dell XPS 13 (2026) - Operating System - Windows 11 Home or Pro - CPU - Up to Intel Core Ultra 7 355, 8 cores, up to 4.7GHz - GPU - Integrated Intel Graphics - RAM - Up to 32GB LPDDR5x, up to 9600 MT/s Dell's latest XPS 13 is its smallest XPS yet. Packing the Core 5 or Core Ultra 7 processors and up to 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM, this ultra-compact laptop is perfect for your day-to-day tasks.

item.title: Ray-Ban Meta glasses update makes them more useful on the go
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.24
What you need to know - Meta AI glasses v28 update adds pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, expanded language support, and camera anti-tampering improvements. - With hands-free walking directions, you can ask Meta to navigate to nearby destinations, with driving directions sent to your phone for farther trips. - Spatial Audio makes listening richer and adds a more immersive layer to music and podcasts on supported Ray-Ban Meta glasses. Meta has been steadily expanding what its AI glasses can do, and the latest v28 update adds several practical upgrades, including pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, and broader language support. Perhaps the headline addition is pedestrian navigation. You can now ask the smart glasses to guide you on foot to nearby destinations using voice commands such as “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” If you’re farther away, the glasses can send driving directions to your phone. There’s also a new way to begin navigation from your phone: Find a destination in your mapping app, tap Share, and select Meta AI, and navigation will start on your connected glasses. The update also broadens where walking directions work. Meta says it now offers walking directions in the U.S., Puerto Rico, Canada, and some cities across the world. Audio gets an upgrade as well. Now, Spatial Audio can make a more immersive version of the stereo sound you’re already getting, whether that’s music or a podcast. You can find this option in Settings > Audio > Spatial. It works with Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 Optics and the Meta Glasses collection. Meta is also adding Mandarin Chinese (zh_CN) support across Device Controls, calls and messaging, media capture and music controls, Meta AI, and MMAI. Finally, v28 has ongoing anti-tampering improvements to protect the cameras on the glasses. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Earlier firmware releases introduced features like Conversation Focus, which uses the microphones in the glasses to help users hear nearby voices better, and deeper Spotify integration. Similarly, on Reddit, the response is pragmatic, with users mostly praising the glasses for hands-free photos, calls, podcasts, and open-ear audio, while battery life and Meta AI’s limitations remain common complaints. item.title: Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 is shaping up to be Google’s best beta yet
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.71
What you need to know - Android 17 QPR2 has officially hit Platform Stability with Beta 4, meaning APIs are locked and the update is in its final stretch focused entirely on system polish and bug fixes. - Google fixed several Pixel pain points, including overheating, unexpected reboots, gesture navigation, battery-limit charging, Recents, Bluetooth audio, and screen-recording issues. - Hardware support gets attention, too, with fixes for USB-C XR mirroring, 3D smart-glasses displays, and low-light Face Unlock. Google’s Android 17 QPR2 beta cycle is moving into its final stretch. Beta 1 was released on July 20, with Beta 2 following on 3 August and Beta 3 only 11 days later. Now, Beta 4 has arrived with a long list of fixes, and more importantly, Android 17 QPR2 has reached Platform Stability. That milestone means Google has locked the API surface for the release, giving developers a much more stable target for testing apps ahead of the update reaching users more broadly. QPR2 is a pretty small SDK update that has no planned behavior changes, so this build is much more about polish, stability, and fixing things that could make a Pixel frustrating to use. Critical bug fixes And there are a lot of things to fix. As per the changelog, Beta 4 resolves a bug in thermal management that could cause overheating and reboots. Another solution is for the 80% battery limit feature that takes way too long to finish charging the last 2%. Google has also fixed broken gesture navigation and a transparent status bar that could appear after full-screen video with specific display-cutout settings enabled. You'll see that polish in everyday Pixel features as well. The search in the app drawer may stop accepting text input. Bluetooth call audio may be routed incorrectly through the phone speaker. The Recents screen may freeze or visually clip app cards. Google also fixed a bug with screen-recording audio that could cause microphones to be unavailable to apps such as Gboard and Gemini until a reboot. There’s some interesting hardware cleanup, too. Beta 4 brings back screen mirroring for USB-C XR glasses and fixes blank screens in 3D mode for connected smart glasses. It also solved Face Unlock issues in low-light conditions that would take users straight to a PIN. Android 17 QPR2 is also beefing up the protection against call-forwarding scams by limiting some USSD-based forwarding commands and requiring confirmation when users manually dial them. Positive user feedback Reddit users who own Pixels are giving surprisingly positive early feedback. One Pixel 9a owner called Beta 4 the most stable QPR2 build yet, with the lag gone and performance noticeably improved. Another Pixel 8 owner said that the phone now feels "fast." Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Beta 4 isn’t perfect, though. Some testers complained about oversized text and a lower display resolution after installing the update, though one user said a reboot fixed everything. At least one tester also states that a Bluetooth routing issue for incoming calls has persisted across all four QPR2 betas, with them having to manually select the Bluetooth audio source. Beta 4 is rolling out to a wide range of Pixel phones and tablets, with Pixel 11 support listed as “coming soon” for now. Some early beta testers on Reddit said a download of about 671MB on a Pixel 9 Pro XL, with a few rollout quirks and some confusion on the update screen. If you're already a Pixel owner and are enrolled in the beta, you'll get the update over the air. Just know that if you leave the program after installing Beta 4, it can wipe your data. item.title: Samsung is shutting down a couple of apps; vows to return new and improved
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.69
What you need to know - Samsung is alerting users about its preparations to shut down the Quick Measure and AR Doodle apps on December 31, 2026. - While Samsung acknowledges "inconveniences" from this, it states that it's "committed" to returning these apps "with improved services" in the future. - In July, Samsung officially axed its Messages app, which has been replaced by the Google Messages app. Samsung is preparing to shut down two apps, and it's delivering warnings to users in preparation for what's to come. Very early this morning (Sept 7), Tarun Vats on X noticed new warnings from Samsung about two apps that are being phased out. Samsung says that it will shut down the Quick Measure app on December 31, 2026. It adds, "After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it's already downloaded, but be aware that some features may not function properly." The Quick Measure app currently works with Google's Wear OS. However, after this termination date from Samsung, it says app support will no longer be provided for new Wear OS versions. Quick Measure isn't the only app getting the boot. Users replying to Vats' thread on X mentioned Samsung's AR Doodle is also getting axed come December 31. A similar warning to users was given for AR Doodle. The date remains the same; however, it swaps Wear OS for regular OS, as this app likely relies on Android/One UI updates. While Samsung recognizes that shutting down an app can cause "inconveniences," the news isn't all bad. Samsung says, "We are committed to returning with improved services in the future." It's not clear if Quick Measure and AR Doodle will return upgraded, new, and improved. Or if we'll see brand-new variations that change these older systems. Another app got shutdown this summer Not going to lie, I had to dig pretty far back to even find anything about Quick Measure. Not sure how many people are going to miss the feature, but I'm there are some out there. It's interesting, considering everything the Samsung Health app can do today. If Samsung is committed to returning in some revamped form, I wonder if these features would find new lives inside existing, supported apps, rather than standalone gigs. If you're confused about "Quick Measure," we wouldn't blame you. Our earliest coverage dates back to 2021, when Samsung rolled out new features for its S Health app (yeah... S Health). That update coincided with the company's Gear Fit 2 launch. Quick Measure let users check their heart rate without launching the full app. Our coverage read, "Simply activate Quick Measure, and you'll now be able to place a finger on the heart rate sensor and wait for a reading." We've come a long way with heart rate tracking and the like related to cardiovascular health. Anyway, the last app shutdown from Samsung was its Messages app in July. Google Messages was reported to be the company's official replacement for users to text. However, consumers with Android 11 and under "are unaffected, and emergency calls still work after the shutdown." item.title: Rakuten Kobo's major in-store e-reader expansion at Best Buy makes it so easy to shop
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.68
What you need to know - Rakuten Kobo is bringing its e-readers to stores for the first time, and it's doing so with 500 Best Buy shops across the U.S. - Consumers can shop the Kobo Clara Colour, Clara BW, Libra Colour, Kobo Stylus 2, and Kobo Remote. - Online availability for these Rakuten Kobo products remains on kobo.com, Staples, Target, and more. If you've ever wanted to physically shop Rakuten Kobo products, you're getting your wish. Today (Aug 27), Rakuten unveiled its newest partnership with a major retailer across the U.S. A press release states Rakuten Kobo e-reader products are heading to 500 Best Buy stores across the U.S. This will be the first time that consumers can shop in stores for Rakuten Kobo products. Previously, as the company highlights in its post, consumers could only shop online for these e-readers. To complement the retailer expansion, Rakuten Kobo's CEO, Michael Tamblyn, said, "Many readers want to be able to pick up a device, see the screen, and feel it in their hands before they commit. With Kobo eReaders now available at Best Buy, more American customers can do just that." Coming to Best Buy stores will be the Rakuten Kobo Clara Colour and Kobo Clara BW. Both devices are "compact and waterproof." What's more, consumers can shop the expansive Kobo Libra Colour. Rounding out Rakuten Kobo's retail expansion are the Kobo Stylus 2 and the Kobo Remote accessories. While it's nice to actually see and envision how these tablets would look in your hands in a cozy chair, Rakuten Kobo says there's more to experience. After purchasing, the post states each e-reader provides access to the Kobo Store and Kobo Plus. The former lets you shop for new books to read, while the latter is a subscription service. Kobo Plus offers a selection of packages with "support for a wide range of eBook formats, and an industry-leading experience for borrowing eBooks directly from local public libraries with Libby and OverDrive." More e-readers hit Best Buy I think I'll always enjoy reading a physical book the most, but e-readers have continued to grab my attention. The idea of buying a book and not having to wait for it to ship or get delivered is nice. I can hop right in, cozy up in a comfortable place, and enjoy myself. Rakuten Kobo understands that sometimes, you need to see (and feel) the device you're interested in. It helps takes the guesswork out an important purchase. We covered Rakuten Kobo's launch of the Libra Colour and Clara Colour. These tablets feature E Ink's Kaledio 3 module screens with stronger processing and improved battery capacities. The Libra Colour, which is what consumers can find in-store at Best Buy, features a 7-inch display, 32GB of storage, and full support for the Kobo Stylus 2. Another highlight of the Libra Colour is its ergonomic design. Rakuten Kobo worked on its form factor with comfort in mind for longer reading sessions. If you enjoy reading a physical book, the Libra Colour might give you those same vibes—it's just digital. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android For all consumers interested in Rakuten Kobo e-readers, or those curious if their store has any, you can check on Best Buy today. If you prefer the online route, Rakuten Kobo says you can still find its e-readers on kobo.com, Staples, Target, and more. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra with hacking risks in check
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.38
What you need to know - GPT-6 Astra is the first OpenAI model to hit the "critical" cybersecurity threat level, but deployment is moving forward with significant safeguards in place. - It is currently limited to defensive tasks like secure code review. Advanced capabilities like exploit creation are blocked for now, but trusted users in the Daybreak program will eventually get access to complex workflows. - Astra drastically outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, hitting a perfect 100% on ExploitBench and 42.4% on ExploitGym. OpenAI just released GPT-6 Astra, and it’s the company's first model to reach the “critical” threat level in the company’s Preparedness Framework for cybersecurity. Despite these unprecedented security risks, OpenAI is moving ahead with the deployment. That doesn't mean GPT-6 Astra is being rolled out as an unrestricted hacking tool. The version rolling out now will do defensive work such as secure code review and patching, but will not entertain more advanced requests like creating proof-of-concept exploits, OpenAI says. The company adds that it intends to relax some of those restrictions with its Daybreak program for trusted users, ultimately supporting workflows such as vulnerability validation, malware analysis and detection engineering. So, how did we arrive at this point? OpenAI had to severely lock down its development pipelines after the recent mess where rogue AI agents hacked the Hugging Face platform. Astra is a huge step up from GPT-5.6 Sol in capabilities. Massive performance leap In OpenAI’s testing, the new model scored 100% on ExploitBench, compared to 78.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol. It also scored 42.4% on ExploitGym against 30.3% for its predecessor. More worrying, Astra uncovered and took advantage of two new zero-day vulnerabilities in the course of testing, which OpenAI says it is reporting to the appropriate maintainers. OpenAI explains that GPT-6 Astra is built on improvements to pre-training, reinforcement learning, alignment, and computer use. It can run software, surf the web, write code, and complete multistep tasks. OpenAI says its OSWorld 2.0 testing shows it’s about 47% faster per task than GPT-5.6 Sol, while scoring 72.6% vs 65.7%. The company says it has responded with stronger jailbreak resistance, broader monitoring, encrypted model checkpoints, tighter access controls, and misalignment monitoring across tool-using deployments. Astra also outperformed Sol in remaining within authorized boundaries. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android But one big weakness that OpenAI does acknowledge is that it’s actually a lot harder to monitor. Internal testing indicated that GPT-6 can actively influence its own "chain of thought” reasoning to avoid leaving incriminating evidence. In adversarial situations, the model has even sandbagged its performance to fly under the radar and avoid internal monitors. For developers, Astra costs $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, with an accelerated API at twice the normal price. It’s rolling out now to a limited number of people before it’s available to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users and the API and Amazon Bedrock.
