item.title: Steam, UV Lights, and Record-Setting Suction: The Most Cutting-Edge Robot Vacuums at IFA 2026
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.60
For years, IFA was a playground for wild, flashy robot vacuum and mop experiments—think elevating chassis and stair-climbing attachments. But at IFA 2026, the category is finally growing up. Instead of headline-grabbing gimmicks, this year's standout bots double down on what actually matters: raw cleaning power and practical mopping upgrades. They might look less radical, but these real-world improvements make this year's lineup the most exciting generation of robot vacuums we've seen yet. Below, we’ve rounded up our favorite robot vacuums from the show floor, along with pricing and release dates where available. iRobot Roomba Max 875 The iRobot Roomba Max 875 has a simple skirt that lowers from the chassis onto the carpet as it cleans. This skirt creates a temporary seal to help focus airflow on extra-stubborn dirt. The feature is called SealForce, and it's a practical change that could make a huge difference in the most important quality of a robot vacuum: cleaning power. Upright and cordless vacuums have long used seals to aid suction, but robot vacuums haven’t; instead, prioritizing mobility, efficiency, and battery life. A movable skirt could strike a balance between the category's needs and more closely match manual machines in fine-particle pickup. Aside from SealForce, the Roomba Max 875 cleans with an impressive 35,000 Pascals of suction and 20 liters per second of airflow. Its self-cleaning roller mop scrubs with 18 newtons of downward pressure while spinning at 300 rotations per minute. A nozzle in front of the roller sprays steam to loosen stains. The mop even retracts into the chassis, which extends a cover over it to eliminate contact with carpets. The base empties the dustbin and washes and dries the mop. The Roomba Max 875 marks a return to innovation for iRobot, and I can't wait to test it. It’s available now for $1,199. Roborock Qrevo Edge 3 Pro and Saros 20 Flow Complete Roborock’s new vacuums take a more direct approach to increased cleaning power. They don’t have any kind of special trick; they just have a staggering amount of suction. Both the Qrevo Edge 3 Pro and the Saros 20 Flow Complete have a record-setting 36,000Pa of suction power. Both can also elevate over taller thresholds than ever before, thanks to AdaptiLift Chassis 3.0, which can lift as high as 3.5 inches. I’m more excited about the Saros 20 Flow Complete, which doesn’t yet have a price or a firm release date in the US, but it will finally bring a self-cleaning roller mop to Roborock’s lineup of vacuums. The mop will exert 15N of downward pressure while spinning at 240RPM, and similar mops have performed exceptionally well in testing. The Qrevo Edge 3 Pro is available now for $1,499.99 and is the company’s shortest model to date, at just 3.13 inches tall. It does have a navigation tower jutting from the top, but that tower can retract when the bot needs to squeeze under furniture and clean hard-to-reach areas. Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV The Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV vacuums with 30,000Pa of suction and mops using a self-cleaning roller mop that washes itself with 158-degree Fahrenheit water. Aside from its suction power and design, the R3 increases its cleaning potency with vision and smarts. It has the same green laser to detect invisible dust as the existing Dyson Spot+Scrub AI, and adds a UV light to detect invisible stains. Specifically, UV light can reveal dried substances like alcohol, milk, and even urine that can be hard to spot once dry. Shark has a similar UV light on its latest flagship model, the PowerDetect UV. In addition to the R3, the R2 Nurovi is a Costco exclusive that has spinning triangular mop pads to better clean corners. The R1 Nurovi is a vacuum-only bot with an angled side sweeper to precisely move dust from along walls and corners and into the path of the vacuum. The R3 is slated to go on sale in the US on Sept. 15 for $1,199. The $699 R2 and the $549 R1 will also come to the US market. Ecovacs Deebot X12S The Ecovacs Deebot X12S has a chamber designed specifically for dust mites. It pushes down into the carpet instead of riding along the top. Aside from the dust-mite chamber, the X12S has a privacy shield that can cover the navigation camera's lens. It also has a self-cleaning roller mop, a base station that washes and dries the mop, and a quick-charge feature that recharges the vacuum during pit stops. It’s available now for $1,299.99. Eufy Omni E35 The Eufy Omni E35 also targets dust mites with a potent 35,000Pa of suction and received certification from the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America for its success in removing dust mites and cat allergens from carpets and hard floors. The roller mop cleans itself as it works and uses water hot enough to eliminate over 99% of bacteria. It also has a Heavy Stain mode that soaks the area during mopping to loosen stuck dirt. The mop itself applies 16N of downward pressure, and the base washes and dries it after the run. The Omni 35 is now available for preorder at $1,299.99. Narwal Freo 20 Edge Narwal’s flagship Flow series extends the side of the mop cylinder that touches the ground, so more is in contact with the floor at once. The company introduced two new models with this tech at IFA, called the FlowWash Mopping System. Available starting September 7, the $799.99 Freo 20 Edge has 31,000Pa of suction for vacuuming, and the base station empties the dustbin and washes and dries the mop after each run. It also has a slim 3.7-inch height to fit under furniture, and can extend the mop to the side to clean along walls and in corners. Dreame Aqua20 Pro Ultra Roller X Complete Dreame’s latest robot vacuum-and-mop hybrid features a roller mop and steam tech similar to the Roomba Max 875. Only, it heats the steam to a piping-hot 356 degrees Fahrenheit before spraying it onto stains through four vents and cleaning it up with a mop that applies 18N of downward pressure and spins at 300RPM. The mop also extends far to the side to scrape away dirt along walls, and its navigation system can recognize 320 different types of obstacles. A North America release date hasn't yet been announced. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Dell 16S Review: A Well-Rounded Daily Driver With a Sprawling OLED Screen
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.52
Dell's 16S ($1,549.99 to start; $1,649.99 as tested) carries a heftier cost than a typical mainstream laptop, but it gives you plenty of bang for the bigger bucks. Sitting below Dell's flagship XPS line, it combines a sturdy metal chassis, a crisp and colorful OLED display, long battery life, and practical connectivity in a very attractive package. While its higher-end configurations are outclassed by Acer’s Swift 16 AI and Asus’ Zenbook A16 (our Editors' Choice pick for big-screen laptops), the lower-cost versions of the 16S deliver a well-rounded laptop for work, school, and entertainment. The 16S delivers the biggest value at the entry level. The basic packages provide all the performance most of you will need: a choice of Core Ultra 5 322 (six cores, up to 4.4GHz) or Core Ultra 7 355 (eight cores, 4.7GHz) processors, 16GB of LPDDR5X memory, and 512GB or 1TB of solid-state storage. If you're hungry for more power, you can upgrade to a 16-core Core Ultra X7 358H or Core Ultra 9 386H, both of which boost the memory to 32GB. The X7 model also adds Intel Arc B390 graphics, but gamers shouldn't get too excited: The souped-up laptop remains geared toward content creation and light gaming, not high-fidelity play. Our test unit carried a $1,649.99 price tag, a palatable total considering the laptop’s OLED display and premium build quality. However, the value proposition becomes a lot muddier when you step up from there: The 16-core CPUs will run you more than $2,000, a price point where competing laptops include even more premium features and performance. Also, bear in mind that the 16S carries a big caveat if you're planning to upgrade down the road. The SSD, battery, and wireless card are user-serviceable—so far, so good—but the memory is soldered and can’t be upgraded. Dell gave the 16S a welcome visual overhaul from the outgoing Dell 16 Plus, selling it in Frost Blue or the darker Celestial Blue finish seen on my review sample. While the design remains conservative, that’s part of the appeal: It looks more premium than a budget laptop but not enough to feel like a luxury purchase. Our touch-equipped test configuration comes in weighing 4.1 pounds (non-touch models are a trimmer 3.9 pounds), making the model heavier than Acer’s Swift 16 AI. The 16S makes up for that added chunk with a sturdy metal chassis that resists flex impressively well. Yes, a 16-inch laptop isn’t ideal for travel, but the 16S’ 0.61-inch profile and 14-by-9.9-inch footprint are about as compact as laptops this size get. Dell’s well-rounded connectivity includes two Thunderbolt 4 ports—the 65-watt power adapter connects to either one—two USB-A connections rated for 5Gbps, HDMI 2.1, and an audio jack. Networking includes Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. As an everyday laptop, it’s hard to find fault with this Dell. Its 16-inch display gives you ample room for multitasking, while the keyboard and touchpad come through on comfort, making long work sessions feel effortless. Combined with its lengthy battery life and broad port selection, the laptop works just as well off the plug as it does on a desk. My unit's 2,880-by-1,800 OLED touch display is easily one of its best features. Its colors look rich, its contrast is deep, and the 120Hz refresh rate lends everyday tasks a smoother feel. Reflections from the glossy touch surface can be distracting outdoors or around overhead lighting, but it’s a worthwhile compromise given the display’s quality. Dell also sells 1,920-by-1,200 and 2,560-by-1,600 IPS panels, but OLED delivers the best visuals. Dell’s keyboard and touchpad are both comfortable and effective. The board delivers satisfying key travel and cushioning, and throws in a number pad that's especially handy if you're doing spreadsheet work. White backlighting provides easy visibility in the dark. The top-hinged mechanical touchpad is another plus, needing just the right amount of pressure for physical clicks. The system's full-range speakers and quality webcam provide a further sense of refinement, a clear step above what you’d find in a budget laptop. My only unanswered wish is for a webcam privacy shutter. I tested the Dell 16S with an eight-core Core Ultra 7 355 processor, integrated Intel Graphics, 16GB of LPDDR5-7467 memory, and a 1TB SSD. This midrange configuration is well-equipped for modern productivity, including office work and streaming. During testing, it kept pleasantly quiet and never became uncomfortably warm. For performance comparison, I included Acer’s Swift 16 AI ($1,799.99 as tested), our $1,999.99 Asus Zenbook A16 review configuration, the Framework Laptop 16 ($3,198 as tested), and our $969.99 Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11 test build. Most of those systems will likely outclass the Dell’s CPU, particularly the Asus’ Snapdragon X2 Elite silicon, but 16S should at least prove competitive with the Snapdragon Plus-equipped IdeaPad. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The 16S showed its limits on these benchmarks. Intel’s mainstream Core Ultra chip posted a respectable PCMark 10 score, easily clearing our 4,000-point baseline for productivity-focused laptops, but it trailed the others in the CPU-focused tests. The 16S proved competitive, if just, with the IdeaPad’s Snapdragon X2 Plus, but lagged several steps behind the rest of the field, especially the Asus’ Snapdragon X2 Elite. As noted, if you want more performance, you can purchase the 16S with Core Ultra H-class CPUs, though even with a Core Ultra 9, the 16S isn't likely to outrun the Zenbook A16. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. Graphics performance followed a similar pattern, with the 16S clearing the fast-enough bar and then some. It won't replace a gaming laptop, but it's not intended to be one. Framework’s dedicated Nvidia GPU outperformed on these benchmarks, but its base configurations also rely on integrated graphics. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). While it didn't set any endurance records, the 16S delivers top-notch battery life, lasting 18 hours in our rundown. The Zenbook A16 and Swift 16 AI outpaced it by less than an hour each, which isn’t enough of a margin to seriously ding the Dell’s time. The 16S should have the stamina to handle a full workday plus overtime without worrying about its charge. Display quality also proved to be one of the 16S’s biggest strengths. Its OLED panel showed near-complete coverage of the DCI-P3 gamut and notably high brightness for its technology. The top-notch screen, in fact, cleanly separates the 16S from more affordable alternatives. Final Thoughts Dell 16S - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Dell’s 16S stands out for getting far more right than wrong, pairing a premium-feeling chassis with an outstanding OLED display, practical ports, and long battery life. Excitement isn’t its forte, but it remains a smart choice for daily use, entertainment, and schoolwork. Just be careful not to overspend: While the base and midrange models present genuine value, higher-end CPU options push the 16S into a price bracket where Acer’s Swift 16 AI and Asus’ Zenbook A16 present more compelling packages. The latter of those alternatives, the Zenbook A16, holds our Editors' Choice award among big-screen laptops. About Our Expert Computers are my lifelong obsession. I wrote my first laptop review in 2005 for NotebookReview.com, continued with a consistent PC-reviewing gig at Computer Shopper in 2014, and moved to PCMag in 2018. Here, I test and review the latest high-performance laptops and desktops, and sometimes a key core PC component or two. I also review enterprise computing solutions for StorageReview. I work full-time as a technical analyst for a business software and services company. My hobbies are digital photography, fitness, two-stroke engines, and reading. I’m a graduate of the Rochester Institute of Technology.

item.title: Will Former CEO Tim Cook Speak at Apple's Huge Fall Event? PCMag Readers Are Split
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.44
At Apple's big fall event, scheduled for Sept. 9, the tech giant is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, plus its long-awaited foldable, and a next-gen Apple Watch. In addition, this will be the first Apple event with John Ternus as CEO, adding an extra layer of intrigue. In anticipation of the "Surprise and Shine" event, we recently ran the third and final round of our Big Guessing Game, in which we asked you to weigh in on what you expected to go down on Sept. 9. (The prize is a new Apple Watch.) Read on to see what our readers predict. Will Tim Cook Speak (or Even Appear) at the Big Event? After 15 years as CEO of Apple, Tim Cook handed the reins over to Ternus on Sept. 1. Cook is not out of the picture, however: He is now the executive chair of Apple's board of directors and is expected to maintain the company's relations with the White House. But will Cook speak, or even appear for that matter, at Wednesday's event? Our readers are split. We asked what you anticipated Cook's level of involvement at "Surprise and Shine" would be. Interestingly, 27% of readers think he'll be a no-show, while 16% believe he'll be there but not speak. However, just over half (57%) say Cook will both appear and speak. What Can We Expect From the New iPhones and Apple Watches? Phones have been getting more expensive lately due to tariffs and the RAM crisis, and Apple has demonstrated it is not immune to raising prices on its products. We asked our readers what the new iPhone Pro model's starting price would be closest to, and they are fairly evenly split among the four options: 27% guess the lowest price we mentioned ($1,200), and 21% think it will be the highest amount ($1,500). Meanwhile, 26% say $1,300, and the same percentage say $1,400. Apple's entire 2025 iPhone lineup uses traditional graphite-based lithium-ion batteries, but might some of the brand's new phones feature silicon-carbon batteries, which can pack far more energy-carrying ions into the same space? After all, Samsung recently adopted silicon-carbon technology for the batteries in the Galaxy Z 8 series. According to one-quarter of our readers, none of Apple's new phones will feature silicon-carbon batteries, though the same percentage says such batteries will be included in three or more of them. About 32% foresee silicon-carbon batteries in exactly two new Apple phones, while 18% think they will be in just one. Speaking of batteries, we also asked about the advertised battery life for the new base Apple Watch. Eighteen percent think the device will have the same 24-hour battery life as the Apple Watch 11. A whopping 77% think it will be more, while just 5% think the charge will dip below a full day. Will Any New AirPods Announced at Apple's Event Have Cameras? Finally, we asked our readers if any new AirPods announced at Apple’s 2026 fall event will have cameras. Last month, Apple accidentally leaked its upcoming camera-equipped AirPods in a video in macOS 26.7. However, according to anonymous sources subsequently cited by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple won’t release a new version of its earbuds until 2027. If Gurman's report is accurate, the 27% of our readers who say no new AirPods will be released this year are correct. Meanwhile, 35% think there will be new AirPods with cameras announced on Wednesday, and 38% say that there will be AirPods announced, just without cameras. Curious to see how accurate our readers' predictions are? Apple's fall event will be livestreamed from the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino beginning at 10 a.m. PT on Sept. 9. And, of course, visit us here at PCMag, where we'll be bringing you all the Apple news as it happens. About Our Expert I'm the Executive Editor, Features & Special Projects at PCMag.com. I oversee both traditional features and the wide variety of editorial packages we run, including the Readers' Choice/Business Choice awards and holiday gift guides. I am an adjunct assistant professor at Columbia Journalism School. Prior to PCMag, I was on staff at BuzzFeed News, Input, BreakerMag, and Blender. In addition, I have written for The New Yorker, The New York Times Magazine, The Washington Post, Wired, WSJ. Magazine, and Rolling Stone, and am the author of Everybody Loves Our Town: An Oral History of Grunge, a Time magazine book of the year. Check out my personal website for examples of my work.

item.title: Report: Tim Cook Won't Be Speaking at Apple's Sept. 9 Event
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.36
Apple is set to hold its first major event under new CEO John Ternus on Wednesday, and one question that intrigues everyone, including us, is whether former CEO Tim Cook will speak. Per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Cook will be in the audience while the video presentation plays, but he won’t be part of the video itself. “Apple has carefully orchestrated this transition to make Ternus the face of the foldable iPhone and all the new products to come. Putting Cook in the presentation would just undermine that.” Gurman says. “So, no, Cook will not be in the video. When it comes to product introductions, it’s the John Ternus era.” Since Gurman is a reliable source for all things Apple, his report pours cold water on the hopes of 57% of our readers who voted in our poll that Cook would both appear and speak. 27% of our readers said he wouldn’t appear at all, and only 16% aligned with Gurman’s view that Cook will appear but not speak. It’s the beginning of a new era at Apple. After 15 years at the helm, Tim Cook stepped down as CEO on Sept. 1 and transitioned into the role of Executive Chair of the Board of Directors. Cook will now “engage with policymakers around the world,” according to Apple, while Ternus handles all product development. How the new approach pans out for Apple remains to be seen. Salary-wise, Ternus will receive a base pay of $3 million for the 2027 fiscal year, while Cook receives $2 million. Adding stock packages, Ternus’ compensation could rise to $58 million for the upcoming year, while Cook’s goes up to $47 million. What to Expect from Apple’s Sept. 9 Event? Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event on Sept. 9 is expected to feature John Ternus delivering a keynote for the first time. The presentation will most likely unveil the first-ever foldable iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12, the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and new AirPods. There have also been rumors about updates to the HomePod and the Apple TV set-top box, but the chances of them being squeezed into an event that’s already packed with major releases seem slim. If introduced, the iPhone Ultra foldable will undoubtedly become the biggest talking point of the event. PCMag will be covering the event from the ground live, and you can watch Apple’s presentation on YouTube from 10 a.m. PT/ 1 p.m. ET. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Asus TUF Gaming A14 (2026) Review: No Discrete GPU? No Problem
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.33
Depending on your perspective, the Asus TUF Gaming A14 (2026) is either a perfectly cromulent gaming laptop or a bleeding-edge proof of concept. On the surface, the TUF Gaming A14 ($2,199.99) delivers potent productivity performance and decent (if inconsistent) gaming performance in a compact, lightweight package. Dig a little deeper, though, and you'll find what makes this device equal parts impressive and unusual: It poses as a gaming laptop, but it has no discrete graphics processor. That makes a big difference, since an integrated graphics processor (IGP) means less noise, less weight, and a longer battery life. The picture isn't entirely sunny, though: This Asus laptop doesn't have the brightest screen, nor will it deliver the fastest frame rates you can find. The Razer Blade 14 (2025) holds our hearts as the best portable gaming laptop, but you'll still find a lot to like about the TUF Gaming A14, particularly if you can live without an OLED screen and can find our test model at a discount. (The pricing is steep if you pay MSRP.) At the time of writing, Asus sells just one TUF Gaming A14 configuration in the US: our review unit, the FA401EA-DS96. It comes packed with an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 392 CPU, integrated AMD Radeon 8060S Graphics, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB PCI Express NVMe SSD. Asus lists this configuration for $2,199.99, although we saw it for $1,999.99 at Best Buy and even lower from Amazon, on occasion. Asus also lists a TUF Gaming A14 configuration, the FA401GM, with a discrete Nvidia GPU. That one features an AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 CPU, an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, up to 32GB of LPDDR5X-7500 memory, and up to a 2TB PCIe NVMe SSD. But you can't get that model in the US just yet, and Asus hasn't provided a hard release date, pricing, or specific configuration options. We can guess at the price point, though: A version with 32GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD costs approximately $3,000 in Japan, so the GeForce-equipped option may also be pricier than our review model if and when it comes stateside. At first glance, looking past the name, you might not realize that the TUF Gaming A14 is a gaming laptop at all. Its plain, dark-gray chassis would look right at home on a standard productivity machine. Pick it up, though, and you'll notice a big distinction: Without a discrete GPU to house, the laptop proves to be surprisingly thin and light, at 0.67 inch thick and 3.26 pounds. For comparison, the Razer Blade 14 is a sliver more svelte (0.64 inch) but also a bit heftier (3.60 pounds), while the Acer Predator Triton 14 AI is bigger all around (0.93 inch, 3.50 pounds). I used the TUF Gaming A14 as my go-to machine for about a week and came away impressed with its portability. The laptop fit in my backpack with plenty of room to spare and didn't weigh me down. I could set up shop anywhere I could find a hard surface and some Wi-Fi. In fact, as I write this review, I am working on the TUF Gaming A14 in a crowded café, and I have enough room in front of me for the laptop, a wireless mouse, and a glass of iced coffee. Using an IGP also helps the TUF Gaming A14 run quietly. While I heard the fans going when I played games, the machine was nearly silent for everyday productivity work and video streaming. Fan noise may not be a make-or-break consideration in a gaming rig, but the silence helped me focus during demanding work assignments and late-night writing sessions. The TUF Gaming A14 also has all the ports you need for gaming gear. Along the left edge, you'll find a proprietary power connection, an HDMI output, a USB Type-C port (with DisplayPort 2.1 and Power Delivery 3.0), a USB Type-A connection, and a 3.5mm audio jack. On the right, you get additional USB-A and USB-C ports, plus a microSD card reader. I was able to hook up an external mouse, a keyboard, a headset, and a display, and I still had a port or two to spare. Here we get to one of this system's drawbacks. While the TUF's size, weight, and general performance make it an excellent productivity tool, its 14-inch, 2,560-by-1,600-pixel screen doesn't match up. Even at maximum brightness, the 165Hz IPS display looks a bit dim, and the colors appear muted. The pinks, reds, and yellows of the default wallpaper should look striking and vibrant, but they blend into each other far too easily. Whether I was looking at photos, watching videos, or playing games, the colors never jumped out the way they should on a machine at this price. The keyboard, on the other hand, pops for both productivity and gaming. With 1.7mm of travel, the keys feel comfortable and responsive, while a bright white backlight makes them easy to see in the dark. You can control the lighting patterns with the Asus Armoury Crate software, though it is arguably more trouble than it's worth. The program gives you a jumble of optional features that can mess with default Windows settings. You can also install the MyAsus and Asus GlideX software packages for even more system updates and file-sharing options, but it can be confusing to figure out how the three programs work together (or don't). I found it easier to uninstall them and let Windows 11 handle performance and update settings. Otherwise, the TUF Gaming A14's built-in audio and visual components work well enough. The speakers pushed a pleasant, balanced soundscape, whether I was listening to Vivaldi while working or Cyberpunk 2077 while relaxing afterward. The 1080p webcam and built-in microphone make for decent video calls, although I'd still recommend a headset with a microphone for conversations where voice quality really counts. The TUF Gaming A14 is also a certified Microsoft Copilot+ PC, offering more advanced Copilot AI features than a standard Windows 11 rig. I used Copilot+ mostly for its enhanced Windows search, which let me find specific settings with general queries (for example, "Change the brightness on my screen" rather than navigating through the Display and Brightness menus). Otherwise, Copilot+ PCs can handle resource-heavy AI tasks, such as live translations and Windows Studio Effects, more effectively than standard Windows 11 builds. The most interesting thing about the TUF Gaming A14 is the silicon. It promises a full-fledged gaming setup without a discrete GPU, leaning instead on the Ryzen CPU's integrated AMD Radeon 8060S Graphics. While most IGPs can handle lightweight, classic, and indie games, the TUF can also tackle big-budget modern fare. That's an impressive feat, but the TUF's actual performance proved to be a mixed bag: The laptop scored well on our productivity benchmarks, while its graphics and gaming results often fell short of its competitors. If you want a light laptop that works well for both productivity and gaming, the TUF Gaming A14 delivers. If you want a gaming laptop first and foremost, though, it may not be the smartest choice. For close competitors, we've chosen the best-in-category Razer Blade 14 ($2,699.99 as tested), the Acer Predator Triton 14 AI ($2,499.99 as tested), the Asus TUF Gaming F16 ($1,299.99 as tested), and the Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10 (about $2,300 as tested). Most of these machines have similar components and screen sizes. The one exception is the TUF Gaming F16, which has a larger screen, less memory, and a smaller SSD, but comparable performance in some areas. All but the TUF Gaming A14 have discrete GPUs. We've also included some anecdotal comparisons with the Asus Zenbook Duo (2026) ($2,699.99 as tested) to see how AMD's most advanced IGP stacks up to Intel's, in its latest "Panther Lake" mobile chip. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess with a variety of automated operations in the seminal image editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The TUF Gaming A14 scored at or near the top in every one of our productivity tests. It came in first for the standard PCMark 10 test—beating out even the Razer Blade 14—and took top marks on our PugetBench/Adobe Photoshop test. Given its promising benchmark results and sleek design, itinerant content creators may consider the TUF Gaming A14 for graphic design and video work. Otherwise, the TUF took second place in the PCMark 10 Storage, Cinebench multi-core, HandBrake, and Geekbench multi-core tests, often by close margins. While the laptop didn't do quite as well on the Cinebench single-core benchmark, it proved a potent productivity performer overall. My qualitative tests backed up these numbers. I used the TUF Gaming A14 for writing, research, and slideshow creation, usually with a dozen tabs open in Chrome and Spotify streaming in the background. The laptop handled all of these tasks without any lag or slowdown, and I could switch among them almost instantaneously. We challenge all tested systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two we use, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), stress the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development, like Metal and DirectX 12, to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last, we turn to Solar Bay to measure ray tracing performance. Our real-world gaming testing is based on in-game benchmarks for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and F1 2024. These three games—all benchmarked at the system’s full HD (1080p or 1200p native) resolution—represent competitive shooters, open-world games, and simulations, respectively. If the screen supports a higher resolution, we rerun the tests at the QHD equivalent of 1440p or 1600p. Each game is run at two sets of graphics settings per resolution, for up to four runs total. We run the Call of Duty benchmark at the Minimum graphics preset—aimed at maximizing frame rates to push display refresh rates—and again at the Extreme preset. Our Cyberpunk 2077 test settings aim to push PCs to the max, so we run it on the Ultra graphics preset and again at the all-out Ray Tracing Overdrive preset without DLSS or FSR. Finally, F1 2024 represents our DLSS effectiveness (or FSR on AMD systems) test, demonstrating a GPU’s capacity for frame-boosting upscaling technologies. We were eager to put the integrated AMD Radeon 8060S Graphics through its paces here. The most important takeaway: A gaming laptop with an IGP sometimes can keep pace with its discrete-GPU competitors. But much of the time, the discrete GPUs still showed an edge; it depends heavily on the specific game. The TUF Gaming A14 earned the top score among its competitors in our 3DMark Wild Life benchmark by a fairly wide margin—but that's the only test where it took first place. In Wild Life Extreme and Solar Bay, it placed around the middle, while it slumped toward the bottom in Steel Nomad and Steel Nomad Light. The TUF stuck to the same pattern in our real-world game benchmarks, finishing last or second-to-last in most of our F1 2024 tests, with or without AMD FSR active. Similarly, the only Cyberpunk 2077 where the Asus didn't come in last was our high-resolution Ray Tracing Overdrive run, where it ran at an unplayable 3 frames per second. (The other systems we tested ran at 2 fps.) However, the TUF surprised us by performing superbly in all of our Call of Duty: Modern Warfare III benchmarks. It earned first place in each instance, even beating the runner-up Razer Blade 14 by more than 30fps on the two low-settings tests. Modern Warfare III is a demanding title, especially with the settings turned all the way up, so it suggests the Radeon 8060S Graphics got some significant help here from the Ryzen AI Max+ 392 CPU, which didn't play out the same way in other games and with COD at higher detail settings. In my anecdotal testing, the TUF Gaming A14 showed both promise and limitations. I could run high-end games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Avowed at high resolutions and see smooth enough frame rates, but only with textures and other graphical settings dialed down to medium. I was never disappointed with how the games ran, but I was never bowled over, either. It's also worth noting that the Radeon 8060S appears to outperform the Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics (found in Intel's Panther Lake Core Ultra X7 and X9 chips) across the board. The TUF Gaming A14 scored higher than the Asus Zenbook Duo (2026) in every graphical and gaming benchmark, save for a single Cyberpunk 2077 Ray Tracing run, where they tied. (The Zenbook Duo we tested uses Intel's Core Ultra X9 388H with the Arc B390.) For the moment, AMD's newest IGP seems more powerful than its Intel counterpart. This is one of the few laptops in which we've seen it deployed, though. We test each laptop's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. In addition, to gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor-calibration sensor and its Windows software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). The TUF Gaming A14 aced its battery test, lasting 12 hours and 52 minutes—very good for a gaming laptop—compared with the Razer Blade 14 (2025)'s 11:37 and the Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10's 5:22. You probably won't see 13 hours of real-world use, but I was able to go a full workday between charges. On the other hand, the TUF doesn't have a particularly bright or colorful screen. While this IPS panel can display 99% of the sRGB color gamut, all of its competitors can hit 100%. No big deal there, but it came in last place for the Adobe RGB and DCI-P3 gamuts with 76% and 77%, respectively, whereas the Razer Blade 14 (2025), Acer Predator Triton 14 AI, and Lenovo Legion 5i Gen 10 were largely at or near 100% with those two gamuts. The TUF also had a dimmer screen than the other laptops, with only 67 nits of brightness at 50% and 179 nits at 100%. Some competitors more than doubled the TUF's score here. Final Thoughts Asus TUF Gaming A14 (2026) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. As a demonstration of the AMD Radeon 8060S, the Asus TUF Gaming A14 is an unqualified success. Asus has successfully produced a gaming laptop that doesn't require a discrete GPU to run modern big-budget games. But even though the machine delivers top-notch design and productivity, it's pretty expensive for a "gaming" laptop without a discrete Radeon RX or GeForce RTX chip. For the moment, gamers seeking a highly portable 14-inch gaming laptop (and who can afford the splurge) may want to stick with the Razer Blade 14 (2025). It doesn't beat the TUF Gaming A14 in every graphical and gaming test, but it delivers more consistent performance across the board, and the screen is much superior. Even so, this Asus experiment is easy to stash in a bag and lasts a long time between charges. For users who want to split the difference between productivity and gaming, the TUF Gaming A14 presents a worthwhile middle ground. Just watch the pricing on this mercurial, unique machine. About Our Expert I've covered science and technology for the past 15 years, with a special focus on gaming hardware. During my career, I've reviewed hundreds of mice, keyboards, headsets, monitors, smartphones, laptops, desktops, and various other gadgets that defy easy categorization. I've also covered some of the industry's biggest trade shows, including the Consumer Electronics Show, E3, IFA, SXSW, and PAX East/West. After starting at The Escapist, my work has appeared in Tom's Guide, Tom's Hardware, Laptop Magazine, LiveScience, Space.com, Scientific American, and Worth Magazine.

item.title: Apple Wants to Wrap Your Room in Sound with New HomePods, Says Leak
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.20
Apple has been part of the smart speaker market since it shipped the original HomePod in 2018. But though users did have the option to hook up two HomePods to play their music in stereo, surround sound (where audio is divided up between four different speakers across a room) has never been on the table as an option. Even if users did happen to own four HomePods and were willing to set it up manually. Now, things could be set to change. According to a trusted Apple leaker, posting on the MacRumors forum, lines of code in the latest audioOS 27 beta reference "tuning files" that interact with speakers in front-left, front-right, rear-left, and rear-right positions. According to pdxfu, in the four-speaker placement, the front speakers will use left- and right-specific audio processing, while the rear HomePods will utilize omnidirectional processing "designed to fill the space behind and around the listener." The code also hinted at a new device on the way. According to the leaker, some of the code references a device that doesn't appear to match any of the currently available HomePods, including the original, 2nd-gen, or HomePod mini. Pdfu says it's impossible to say if this is a reference to a 3rd-gen HomePod or a HomePod mini sequel. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has reported that a HomePod mini successor with new Siri Ai support is expected soon, adding that the hardware has reportedly been ready for months and is expected to launch this fall alongside iOS 27. A new Party Mode could also be on the table. Party Mode, when enabled, will use an audio-rendering mode called diffuse. This means the sound will be spread into "a wider, more ambient mix," which will "fill a room more evenly instead of creating a perfect listening spot in front of the speakers." Apple Insider notes that as the code references new hardware, it's likely we'll have to wait for Apple to release new devices to see these features in action, and Apple still doesn't have anything officially announced yet. About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: These Airport Execs Are All-In on Facial Recognition, But Not Necessarily for the Reasons You'd Think
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.51
Fretting about flight delays, whether the cause is increasingly chaotic weather or an understaffed air-traffic control system, can send your travel anxiety soaring well before you reach cruising altitude. Would you also like to have biometric identity theft on your mind at the terminal? A panel at the Identity Week conference in Washington, DC, invited that question, with panelists praising the potential of biometric authentication to speed “seamless travel.” The three speakers, representing airports in Denver, Miami, and Vancouver, all seemed a bit puzzled why travelers weren’t as sold on this vision as they were. How Much Is Saved Time Worth? “There's a trust issue somewhere,” said Maurice Jenkins, chief innovation officer at Miami International Airport, after observing that he sees more people in the regular TSA Pre lines than in lines for the “Touchless” facial-recognition-based version of Pre. “We need to find out somewhere how [to] fix that.” He and his fellow speakers—Dave LaPorte, chief operating officer of Denver International Airport, and James Snowdon, director of infrastructure and airport applications at the Vancouver Airport Authority—phrased this as a matter of time savings. “We're trying to drive customer satisfaction,” LaPorte said. “The way that we do that is by reducing line waits.” Snowdon chimed in: “Biometric boarding is absolutely the way to go," citing “the throughput gain, the hassle removal for the customer.” For airports, the logic of efficiency at scale is paramount. “It saves seconds per transaction,” LaPorte said, noting that Denver is reaching 83 million passengers a year. “Those seconds compound, and we save a lot of time.” Snowdon summed up the upside as “one more flight, one more turn per day per gate.” Airports also see travelers’ time differently than travelers might. As LaPorte observed, more time after security means more time to spend money in the terminal. Snowdon agreed: “We'd like to see our spend per passenger grow.” For passengers, things can be more complicated. I can attest that Touchless Pre can save a non-trivial amount of time, not because it takes me that much longer to hand over my driver’s license or passport, but because there are fewer people in that line. As in, the thing that Jenkins described as a problem to fix. Transactional Privacy The conversation then turned to non-identity transactions and did not get any more convincing. LaPorte, for example, suggested that passengers could use facial recognition for routine purchases in a terminal: “You could get a cup of coffee.” It’s hard to see the upside for passengers who would have to register a credit card with whatever facial-recognition system they might use when tapping to pay with their phones is fast and familiar. There’s a stronger case for digital IDs stored on phones; at an airport, you would already hold up a phone with a boarding pass without handing over the device in either case. LaPorte argued that digital IDs are safer than physical ones. “First of all, people don't lose their phones like they lose their driver's licenses,” he said, adding that phones lock in a way that wallets don’t. “You've got to have some way to get into the device.” (The conference itself demonstrated the usefulness of phone-bound credentials: I only had to show a QR code emailed to me to collect my press badge Thursday morning.) Snowdon touted Air Canada’s work to let people securely store digital identifications generated from their passports on a device in the airline’s app, although this still requires facial recognition verification at airports. Keeping that ID on the device instead of storing it on a server also avoids scenarios like the massive breach of digital scans of driver’s licenses, apparently first collected during car rentals, cybersecurity reporter Brian Krebs reported Tuesday. Jenkins voiced some frustration about how people are willing to hand over “everything” to Amazon. But the retail giant’s one major venture into biometric security so far, the “palm payments” for Whole Foods and other Amazon-owned stores, remains optional. And while Amazon’s economic influence is enormous, it is still not the government. Should We Talk About the Government? Actual governments, meanwhile, have a lot of explaining to do regarding their handling of people’s digital credentials and data collected by cameras trained on people, including the widespread abuse of data gathered by automated license-plate readers. As press coverage has documented at length, the lax default settings of Flock Safety cameras left them open to abuse, after which departments have often done little to stop that and hold officers accountable. And under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has shown itself all too eager to deploy facial recognition against protesters it has been seeking out not just on the streets but on social media, and, in some cases, to cancel Global Entry memberships for people it has identified. If you’re crossing an international border, things are different: If another country or your own wants to take pictures of you, they can and they will. But for domestic travel, authenticating yourself with your face remains a choice. And “trust us” remains an insufficient argument, especially with the continued lack of any comprehensive federal privacy law. Jenkins seemed to grasp that much: “We want to engage with you and have that conversation, but there is an aversion that you have.” He’s right about that aversion, but the anxieties involved stretch far beyond the ends of any airport’s runways. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Big Time Storage Savings: Labor Day SSD Deals From Samsung, SanDisk, and More

item.title: OpenAI's New Internal 'Research Assistant' Uses AI to Build Better AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.35
OpenAI is celebrating reaching its goal of building an "automated research intern" designed to help accelerate and support future model development. The brand calls this “a system that can carry out well-defined research tasks under human direction, including tasks that would take a skilled researcher a few days.” It intends to ask researchers to use the tool to “further progress on deep learning and alignment, enabling iterative improvements.” In a recent blog post, OpenAI noted how many of its own researchers now use coding agents to speed up their work and handle more complex tasks. Over the last few months, GPT-powered agents have been used for more internal tasks than ever before, freeing up OpenAI's researchers to run more experiments and develop future ideas. CEO Sam Altman first announced the goal of developing an automated researcher last October, setting a deadline of September 2026. Altman also outlined the brand's next step, what he calls an “automated AI researcher", which OpenAI says it's on track to hit. That deadline is March 2028. The blog post confirms that safety is a major concern for OpenAI's latest innovation, freely admitting it doesn’t yet know how to run its ultimate automated AI researcher safely. That’s especially pertinent given ongoing security incidents with other OpenAI tools. This news comes at a time when OpenAI is navigating a series of what it calls “misalignments," including the Hugging Face hack and the recently confirmed incident where autonomous agents edited entries over 15,000 times on the German, Wikipedia-like service DseWiki. OpenAI says, “Whenever we find that proceeding would pose an unacceptable safety risk, we will respond appropriately including by slowing or stopping our development or deployment of systems we find ourselves unable to sufficiently safeguard." Last week, OpenAI introduced its new Astra model, which is now available to subscribers worldwide. The brand called it the "world's most intelligent and aligned model." Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Amazon Cargo Plane Crashes at Miami Airport, Leaving 5 Dead
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.20
An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane crashed while attempting to land at Miami International Airport on Sunday. The plane was being operated by 21Air, and at least five people have lost their lives, Amazon confirmed. “We're heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. In a statement, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the incident occurred at around 2 p.m. ET and that the plane involved was a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft arriving from the Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. Footage circulating on X shows the plane was unstable during landing. It overran the runway and hit a few cars before one of its wings caught fire. Over 200 firefighters arrived at the scene, and the FAA grounded all flights for rescue operations. “At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured,” Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said in a press conference. It’s unclear if those killed were in the cars or on the plane. The pilot and the copilot were trapped in the cockpit, while one person had to be rescued from under a vehicle, the county officials added. The FAA has ordered an investigation. “We're working closely with local authorities and officials to learn more and will cooperate fully with any investigation,” Amazon said. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Dell's September Savings Are Here With Big Deals on Top-Rated Desktops, Laptops, and Monitors
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.71

We rate Dell and its gaming sub-brand Alienware consistently highly, and our reviews back that up year-over-year, benchmarking competitively at good prices. With over four decades of hardware teardowns under our belts, our experts have tested a wide range of tech products, so you can trust that their ratings are clear and unbiased. Dell's online store has September deals on highly-ranked laptops, desktops, and monitors. These eight discounts are worth your time and money. Laptop Deals Dell's laptop offerings hit a number of different niches, but if you want a portable that does just about everything well, the Dell Pro 16 is the one, especially at a discount of nearly $500 off retail. A big 16-inch FHD+ screen is one of the top selling points, making it great for creative work as well as watching movies and TV shows, and the chipset is optimized for Windows Copilot AI functionality, at the tip of your fingers thanks to a dedicated keyboard key to open it up in any context. Check out our write-up of this machine to learn more about its solid port selection and connectivity, durable build, and other strong points. In our review, we gave it an "Excellent" rating, with writer Matthew Buzzi praising its gaming performance and adding that benchmarking tests "proved it to be a snappy laptop for productivity and general use" as well. The New Dell Tower takes all of the features we've come to love and refines them just a little bit, and a $130 price cut makes this model worth your attention. If you're the tinkering type, a removable side panel with tool-less entry gives you quick access to internal components. Port selection is solid both front and back, and it supports Wi-Fi 6 for speedy connectivity. All-in-one PCs are a great midpoint between a laptop and a traditional desktop, and Dell makes a variety of well-reviewed models. We put this one through its paces with a full breakdown, noting that it was best suited to be a general-purpose entertainment device for a household, with its large FHD screen that boasted decent brightness and good viewing angles. In terms of sheer processing power, the Intel Core 5 CPU isn't a record-setter, but it's more than good enough for everyday Internet browsing and light productivity work. We also noted that the 1080p webcam was pretty clear and colorful, so if you're looking for an easy way to Zoom call your grandma, look here. Save $200 at Dell right now. A gaming desktop hitting five figures is pretty wild, but that's just the world that we live in. If you recently came into some cash and want to pick up a battlestation that'll dominate all of the hottest games at peak settings for years to come, you can't do much better than this absolutely overpowered Alienware Area-51. With an RTX 5090 graphics card, you can pump out 4K at massive framerates with all of the new DLSS image smoothing, and 64GB of system memory means that literally nothing can make it lag. We have a full review of this desktop, giving it an "Excellent" rating. In addition to the incredible component loadout, we praised its positive pressure airflow system that kept everything cool as a cucumber even under heavy loads, as well as the case's ease of access, with QR codes giving you simple instructions for opening and modifying. Monitor Deals If you need peak resolution at an off-peak price, this $40 discount on Dell's exceptional 32 Plus monitor is great news. With ComfortView Plus technology, reduced blue light and seamless 120Hz frame rate makes it easy on the eyes for extended periods of time, and the VA panel delivers great visuals with 99% sRGB and 95% DCI-P3 color coverage and a 3000:1 contrast ratio. Port arrangement is also quite good, with side-access HDMI making it easier to connect and remove input sources. The stand is height, tilt, and pivot-adjustable, and the ultra-thin bezel around the screen is barely noticeable. We have a review of a similar-sized Dell monitor (with an OLED display instead of the VA one) and raved about its reasonable price and great built-in speakers.
